The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation
Karpathy — builds autograd from nothing. Two and a half hours that replace a term of lectures.
~150 lines: a scalar autograd engine plus a neural net library on top. Read it in one sitting.
Christopher Olah — the clearest short explanation of why reverse mode beats forward mode, with sum-over-paths diagrams.
Stanford — gradient flow through each primitive, with the staged-computation patterns that avoid mistakes.
Automatic differentiation in machine learning: a survey
Baydin et al. — forward vs reverse mode, cost bounds and checkpointing, in one readable survey.
PyTorch — how the graph is actually built, plus the in-place-operation and saved-tensor rules behind the classic autograd errors.

t: Activations: why ReLU won and what replaced it
sum: Why networks need non-linearity, how sigmoid and tanh saturate, what made ReLU trainable and how units die, and how GELU, SiLU and gated units (SwiGLU) became the feed-forward layer of modern LLMs.
prereq: dl1
Backprop multiplies the incoming gradient by each operation's local slope, so an activation's derivative is a factor in every gradient that passes through it.
ml6
Logistic regression applies a sigmoid to a weighted sum; its gradient with respect to the pre-activation is p − y.
ml5
Cross-entropy on softmax probabilities is the classification loss, and it is paired with the output activation.
why:
In the 1980s and again in the 2000s, researchers stacked more and more layers into neural networks and found the same disappointing thing: past three or four layers, adding depth made training worse, not better. The networks that could be trained were shallow. For years the standard explanation was that deep networks were simply hard to optimise. The real culprit turned out to be small and unglamorous: the shape of a one-line function applied to every neuron, the activation function.

Every neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs and then passes it through such a function. Choose a curve that goes flat at both ends (sigmoid, tanh, the natural choices in the early days) and, as the error signal travels backwards through ten or twenty layers, it is multiplied at each layer by a slope that is nearly zero. The first layers learn nothing. Choose a function whose slope is exactly 1 for positive inputs — ReLU, "if it's positive keep it, otherwise output zero" — and the signal passes through intact. In 2012 that swap was one of the ingredients that let AlexNet win the ImageNet competition by a wide margin, training on two consumer graphics cards; its authors reported reaching a given training error six times faster than with tanh.

The story did not end there, because ReLU has its own failure: a unit that is pushed into the region where it outputs zero gets zero gradient and never comes back. So the field kept iterating — leaky and parametric versions, smooth curves called GELU and SiLU, and finally gated units such as SwiGLU, which sit inside the feed-forward block of essentially every recent large language model. If you open the configuration of LLaMA, PaLM or Gemma, the activation function is one of the first architecture choices listed, and an interviewer expects you to say why it is that one.

This lesson builds the subject from the ground up. We show, with numbers, why a network without a non-linearity is useless and how two ReLU units solve XOR; then why sigmoid and tanh saturate and what that does to gradients; what makes ReLU work and how units die; how GELU and SiLU smooth it; how gated linear units add a multiplicative gate and why they need a third weight matrix and a 2/3 hidden width; which output activation goes with which loss; and how activation and initialisation must be chosen together. The public case is Shazeer's 2020 controlled comparison that moved the industry from ReLU and GELU to SwiGLU, checked against the paper's own table.
body:
1. Why stacking linear layers gets you nothing

Take two layers without activations: h = W1·x and y = W2·h. Substitute: y = W2·(W1·x) = (W2·W1)·x. Matrix multiplication is associative, so the two layers are exactly one layer whose matrix is the product. With numbers: W1 = [[1, 2], [0, 1]], W2 = [[2, 0], [1, 1]], x = (1, 1). Layer by layer: h = (3, 1), y = (6, 4). Combined: W2·W1 = [[2, 4], [1, 3]], and [[2, 4], [1, 3]]·(1, 1) = (6, 4). Same answer. A network of 50 such layers is one matrix, and its decision boundaries are straight lines (or hyperplanes). Adding biases does not change this — affine maps compose into affine maps.

The classic proof that this is a real limitation is XOR: output 1 when exactly one of two inputs is 1. Any affine function f(x₁, x₂) = ax₁ + bx₂ + c satisfies f(0,0) + f(1,1) = f(0,1) + f(1,0) (both sides equal a + b + 2c). XOR would need 0 + 0 on the left and 1 + 1 on the right, so no linear model can compute it. Now add a ReLU. Let h₁ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂), h₂ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂ − 1) and output h₁ − 2h₂:

x₁, x₂x₁+x₂h₁h₂h₁ − 2h₂
0, 00000
0, 11101
1, 01101
1, 12210

Two hidden ReLU units solve a problem no number of linear layers can. The mechanism: ReLU folds the number line at a chosen point, and a weighted sum of folds can make bumps and zigzags. The universal approximation theorem says that with enough such units a network can approximate any reasonable function; the question deep learning cares about is which activation lets us find the weights by gradient descent.

2. What we want from an activation

A good hidden-layer activation should (a) be non-linear, obviously; (b) have a slope that stays around 1 over the range of inputs we actually see, so gradients neither vanish nor explode as they pass back; (c) be cheap, since it runs on every neuron of every layer of every example; (d) be differentiable, or nearly so, because backprop needs a slope; and (e) ideally keep the layer's output at a reasonable scale (roughly centred and not growing without bound) so the next layer sees well-behaved inputs. Each generation of activation trades these against each other.

3. Sigmoid and tanh: smooth, bounded — and they saturate

Sigmoid and tanh were the default for decades because they look like biological neurons ("firing rate between 0 and 1") and are smooth. Their values and slopes:

zσ(z)σ′(z) = σ(1−σ)tanh(z)tanh′(z) = 1 − tanh²
00.5000.2500.0001.000
±10.731 / 0.2690.197±0.7620.420
±20.881 / 0.1190.105±0.9640.071
±40.982 / 0.0180.018±0.9990.001
±50.993 / 0.0070.007±1.0000.0002

The slope of sigmoid is at most 0.25, achieved only at z = 0, and it falls to 0.007 by |z| = 5. Tanh's peak slope is 1 but it, too, collapses: 0.07 at |z| = 2. When a unit's input lands far from zero the unit is saturated — pinned near 0 or 1 (or ±1) — and its slope is almost zero, so a gradient arriving from above is multiplied by a near-zero number and stops. This is the mechanical cause of the vanishing gradient problem, examined in depth in dl3.

The compounding, with numbers. Backprop multiplies one slope per layer (plus the weights). Take the best case for each function and ignore the weights: after k layers the gradient is scaled by 0.25ᵏ for sigmoid. After 5 layers that is 0.001; after 10 layers, 9.5×10⁻⁷. For tanh at a typical |z| ≈ 1 (slope 0.42): 0.013 after 5 layers, 1.7×10⁻⁴ after 10. For an active ReLU path the factor is 1ᵏ = 1. If the first layer's gradient is a millionth of the last layer's, the first layer's weights barely move in any reasonable time, and the network effectively trains only its last few layers.

A second problem: sigmoid is not zero-centred. Its output is always positive. Consider a neuron in the next layer: its weight gradient is ∂L/∂w_j = (upstream gradient) × x_j, where x_j is the sigmoid output feeding it. If every x_j is positive, all the weight gradients for that neuron have the same sign (that of the upstream gradient), so the weights can only all increase or all decrease together in a step. To move in a direction where some go up and others down, the optimiser must zig-zag. Tanh, being centred on zero, avoids this, which is why tanh usually beat sigmoid in hidden layers. Both also need an exponential, which is slow relative to a comparison.

4. ReLU: what changed, and why it worked

ReLU(z) = max(0, z). Its slope is 1 where z > 0 and 0 where z < 0 (at exactly 0 frameworks use 0). Rectifiers were proposed for neural networks by Nair & Hinton (2010) and studied for deep supervised training by Glorot, Bordes & Bengio (2011); AlexNet (2012) made them famous. There are three reasons it works so well.

  • The slope is exactly 1 on active units. The gradient through an active unit passes unchanged, so an active path across a hundred layers does not shrink the signal by activation slopes at all. (Weights still matter — dl3.)
  • It is cheap and sparse. One comparison, no exponential. At initialisation about half of a layer's units output exactly zero for a given input, so information is carried by a sparse subset of active units, and the backward pass for the zeroed units is trivially zero.
  • It is piecewise linear and scale-equivariant. ReLU(c·z) = c·ReLU(z) for c > 0. A network of ReLUs (without biases) scales its output when its input scales, which makes the optimisation landscape better behaved, and inside each region of input space the network is exactly a linear function whose slope is a product of 0/1 gates and weights.

The AlexNet paper's evidence is direct. Its Figure 1 shows that a four-layer convolutional network with ReLUs "reaches a 25% training error rate on CIFAR-10 six times faster than an equivalent network with tanh neurons", and the authors add that they "would not have been able to experiment with such large neural networks for this work if we had used traditional saturating neuron models". Their network had 60 million parameters and trained in five to six days on two GTX 580 GPUs.

5. How a ReLU dies

The price of a slope of exactly 0 on the negative side: a unit whose z is negative for every example in the data outputs 0 and has zero slope, so no gradient reaches its weights or its bias. Nothing can move it back. A worked case: a unit computes z = 1.0·x + b on data with x between 0 and 1. With b = 0.1, z ranges over 0.1 to 1.1: active. Now suppose one large update (a big learning rate, or a rare huge gradient) pushes b to −5. Now z ranges from −5 to −4. The output is 0 for every example; the slope is 0 for every example; ∂L/∂b = ∂L/∂w = 0. The unit is dead, and gradient descent, which only moves parameters in response to gradients, will never revive it. In the lesson's lab, with a learning rate of 3, about 41% of the hidden units in a small ReLU network were silent on all 400 training examples, against 3–6% at moderate learning rates.

A dead unit is not a crash: the loss still falls, using the remaining units. You have simply paid for capacity you do not have. The usual causes are learning rates that are too high, large negative biases, badly scaled inputs, and (with Adam) early steps that are too large; the diagnostic is the fraction of zero activations per layer, logged per step. Remedies:

  • Leaky ReLU (Maas et al., 2013): max(0.01z, z) — a small slope on the negative side so gradient always flows.
  • PReLU (He et al., 2015): the same, but the negative slope is learned. The extra parameters equal the number of channels — negligible — and PReLU networks gave 5.71% top-5 error as a single model and 4.94% as a multi-model result on ImageNet — the first published result to beat the 5.1% error reported for human annotators.
  • ELU (Clevert et al., 2015): z for positive z and α(eᶻ − 1) for negative z — smooth and saturating at −α.
  • Softer training: a smaller learning rate, warmup, and He initialisation (section 8), all of which prevent the big early updates that kill units.

6. GELU and SiLU: smoothing the corner

Transformers moved to smooth ReLU relatives. GELU (Gaussian error linear unit; Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016) is GELU(z) = z·Φ(z), where Φ(z) is the probability that a standard normal random variable is below z. Read it as: multiply the input by the probability that it "wins" against a random threshold. For large positive z, Φ ≈ 1 and GELU ≈ z; for large negative z, Φ ≈ 0 and GELU ≈ 0; near 0 it bends smoothly. SiLU (also called Swish with β = 1; Ramachandran et al. found it by automated search, Elfwing et al. proposed it independently) is SiLU(z) = z·σ(z), which is very close in shape. Values (the drill asks for other points):

zReLUGELUSiLUGELU′(z)
−30−0.004−0.142−0.012
−10−0.159−0.269−0.083
00000.500
110.8410.7311.083
332.9962.8581.012

Three properties are worth knowing. The curve is non-monotonic: GELU dips to a minimum of about −0.170 near z = −0.75 (SiLU to −0.278 near z = −1.28) and then rises back to 0, so small negative inputs give small negative outputs rather than exactly zero. The slope is never exactly zero for moderate negative inputs (−0.083 at z = −1), so a unit cannot die in the ReLU sense — although for very negative z the slope is again tiny (−0.012 at −3). And the slope can slightly exceed 1 (GELU′(1) = 1.083), unlike ReLU. In practice GELU is computed either exactly with the error function or with the tanh approximation 0.5z(1 + tanh(√(2/π)(z + 0.044715z³))), whose worst-case error is about 5×10⁻⁴; the two are interchangeable for training but a checkpoint trained with one should be served with the same one (see prod).

Why smooth? A common argument is that a non-zero, smoothly varying gradient near zero gives the optimiser more information than ReLU's hard 0/1 switch, and that the negative dip lets units carry a little information about how far below the threshold the input is. Honest summary: BERT and GPT-2 used GELU, Swish/SiLU appear in EfficientNet and many vision models, the empirical gain over ReLU is modest (Ramachandran et al. report +0.9% top-1 ImageNet accuracy for Mobile NASNet-A and +0.6% for Inception-ResNet-v2 from swapping in Swish), and no one has a decisive theory. Say so in an interview.

7. Gated linear units and SwiGLU

The most important recent change is not another pointwise curve but a gate. A transformer's feed-forward block (FFN) processes each token vector x of width d: project up to a wider hidden size, apply an activation, project back down.

standard FFN:   FFN(x)    = W2 · f(W1 · x)                       two matrices: W1 (d×4d), W2 (4d×d)
gated FFN:      SwiGLU(x) = W2 · ( SiLU(Wg · x) ⊙ (Wu · x) )      three matrices: Wg, Wu (d×h), W2 (h×d)

In a gated linear unit (GLU; Dauphin et al., 2016) the layer computes two parallel linear projections of the same input — a gate branch and an up (value) branch — passes the gate through an activation and multiplies the two elementwise (⊙). SwiGLU uses SiLU for the gate, GeGLU uses GELU, ReGLU uses ReLU, and the "bilinear" layer uses no activation at all. The gate decides, for every hidden unit and every token, how much of the value to let through: the multiplication makes the effective transformation depend on the input in a way a fixed pointwise curve cannot.

A worked SwiGLU. Take x = (1, 2), gate matrix Wg = [[0.5, −1], [0.5, 0.25]] and up matrix Wu = [[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]. Gate pre-activation: x·Wg = (0.5 + 1.0, −1 + 0.5) = (1.5, −0.5). SiLU: SiLU(1.5) = 1.5 × σ(1.5) = 1.5 × 0.8176 = 1.226; SiLU(−0.5) = −0.5 × 0.3775 = −0.189. Up branch: x·Wu = (1 + 1, 0.5 + 2) = (2, 2.5). Elementwise product: (1.226 × 2, −0.189 × 2.5) = (2.453, −0.472). Now the backward pass, as in dl1: the gradient with respect to the up branch is the gate value (1.226, −0.189) times the incoming gradient — the value path is scaled by how open the gate is — and the gradient with respect to the gate pre-activation is SiLU′ times the up value: SiLU′(1.5) = 1.041, so 1.041 × 2 = 2.083 for the first unit and 0.260 × 2.5 = 0.650 for the second. Each branch's gradient depends on the other branch's value: that is what "multiplicative interaction" means, and why the layer can represent products of features (a bilinear form) that a pointwise nonlinearity of a single projection cannot.

Parameter counting. A standard FFN with hidden width 4d has 2 × d × 4d = 8d² weights. A gated FFN with hidden width h has 3 × d × h. Setting 3dh = 8d² gives h = 8d/3 ≈ 2.67d — "the 2/3 rule", since 2/3 × 4d = 8d/3. For d = 4,096: standard, 2 × 4,096 × 16,384 = 134.2 million weights per layer; gated with h = 10,923, 3 × 4,096 × 10,923 = 134.2 million. In practice h is rounded to a multiple of 256 for hardware efficiency: LLaMA-7B uses 11,008 (3 × 4,096 × 11,008 = 135.3 M). Llama 3 goes further and treats the FFN width as a free hyperparameter: 14,336 for d = 4,096 (about 3.5d), 28,672 for d = 8,192 and 53,248 for d = 16,384, all with SwiGLU. Those are scaling decisions, not consequences of the activation.

Why does gating help? Nobody has a proven answer. Plausible ingredients: the gate gives every hidden unit an input-dependent multiplier (a soft, learned "which features matter for this token" selection), the product creates second-order interactions between features, and the gate branch keeps a healthy gradient path because its non-linearity is applied to one factor while the other passes linearly. Shazeer's paper is honest about it: "We offer no explanation as to why these architectures seem to work; we attribute their success, as all else, to divine benevolence." The evidence is a controlled experiment, which we review in prod.

8. Output activations go with losses

The last layer's activation is chosen from the target, not from fashion. It is always paired with a loss, and in every classification pairing the fused gradient with respect to the logits is p − y (the derivation in dl1, section 6).

TaskOutput activationLoss
Regression (any real number)none (linear)MSE or Huber
Binary classificationsigmoidbinary cross-entropy
Multi-class (one correct label)softmaxcategorical cross-entropy
Multi-label (any subset correct)independent sigmoidsbinary cross-entropy per label
Strictly positive output (rate, scale)softplus or exptask-specific (e.g. Poisson or Gaussian likelihood)
Bounded output in [a, b]scaled sigmoid or tanhMSE

Two practical details. First, use the fused "with logits" loss functions (F.cross_entropy, BCEWithLogitsLoss): they take raw logits and apply the log-sum-exp trick internally, avoiding overflow and the log of a tiny probability. Softmax is pᵢ = e^{zᵢ}/Σⱼe^{zⱼ}; computed naively, logits of 1,000 make e^1000 overflow to infinity. Subtracting the largest logit first changes nothing (softmax is shift-invariant) and makes the largest exponent 0. Second, softmax has a temperature: dividing logits by T > 1 flattens the distribution and T < 1 sharpens it — the knob behind LLM sampling.

9. Activation and initialisation must be chosen together

Initial weights are random; their scale decides whether the signal keeps a steady size as it passes through layers. For a layer with n inputs and weights of variance σ², the output pre-activation has variance about n·σ²·E[x²]. For that to equal E[x²] (a steady scale), we would need σ² = 1/n. But a ReLU sets negative values to zero, which cuts the mean square of its output to half that of its input. To compensate, He et al. (2015) use σ² = 2/n for ReLU networks (He initialisation); Glorot & Bengio's Xavier initialisation, 2/(n_in + n_out), targets roughly symmetric activations like tanh. Measured effect: in a quick experiment with 10 ReLU layers of width 1,000 and unit-variance input, He initialisation kept the root-mean-square activation at 0.95, while the 1/n rule shrank it to 0.031 — exactly 2⁻⁵, because half the second moment is lost at each of ten layers. The signal (and the gradient, which sees the same halving in reverse) fades exponentially. dl3 develops this fully.

deep:
Why a piecewise-linear network is so expressive

A ReLU network computes a function that is linear on each of many polyhedral regions of input space; each hidden unit introduces a hyperplane where its input crosses zero, and the pattern of on/off units identifies the region. Composing layers folds space repeatedly, and Montúfar et al. (2014) showed that the number of distinct linear regions can grow exponentially with depth for a fixed number of units, while it grows only polynomially with width in a shallow network. That is the theoretical case for depth: a deep ReLU net can carve up its input space into astronomically many pieces with a modest number of parameters. Within a region the network is exactly linear, so its gradient is a product of the weight matrices and 0/1 masks — clean, and free of saturation. The cost is zero curvature almost everywhere and hard "corners" in the loss surface.

Activation sparsity and its use for inference

ReLU produces exact zeros; in ReLU-based LLMs (OPT, for example) a large majority of feed-forward neurons are inactive for any given token, and systems work exploits this by skipping the matmul columns for zeroed units ("contextual sparsity"). SwiGLU and GELU models are much less sparse in the strict sense, because their outputs are almost never exactly zero, which is a real trade-off: the quality advantage of gated units is paid for in lost inference sparsity. This is why some efficiency-focused work returns to ReLU or, as in Nemotron-4 15B, uses squared ReLU (max(0, z)², found by architecture search in the Primer paper), which is still exactly sparse but has a smooth, growing slope. When someone asks "why not ReLU in an LLM?", the two-sided answer is quality (gated units win in controlled tests) versus sparsity and simplicity (ReLU-family wins for cheap inference).

Gates, second-order structure and the bilinear layer

The bilinear layer (xW) ⊙ (xV) has no activation at all and still beats ReLU in Shazeer's Table 1 (1.960 versus 1.997 log-perplexity at 65,536 steps). That says much of the benefit is the multiplication: a product of two linear projections computes a quadratic form in x, i.e. pairwise feature interactions, which a single pointwise non-linearity applied to one projection expresses only indirectly. Adding an activation to the gate (SwiGLU, GeGLU) keeps the multiplicative structure and adds a saturating or bending element that keeps values bounded in the gate path, and those variants come out best. A second view: the gate is a per-token, per-unit soft mask, which is the same mechanism as the gates in LSTMs (dl7) and the routing weights of mixture-of-experts layers. Experts in modern mixture-of-experts models are themselves SwiGLU blocks.

Second derivatives, smoothness, and optimisation

ReLU's second derivative is zero except for a delta function at 0, so the Hessian of a ReLU network's loss has curvature contributions only from the layers' weights interacting, never from the activation itself. Smooth activations contribute their own curvature, which matters to methods that use second-order information and to analyses such as sharpness-aware minimisation, where non-smooth activations complicate the theory. For everyday first-order training the practical consequence is small; the more important effect is the non-zero gradient for small negative inputs, which prevents the permanent death of units.

Fusion: why elementwise cost is hidden

An activation is an elementwise operation: it reads a tensor from memory, applies a function, and writes it back. Its arithmetic is negligible next to the matmul that produced its input, but its memory traffic is not: a standalone GELU over a (tokens × 4d) tensor moves two full passes of data through GPU memory, which is slow relative to the compute (the roofline argument of gpu2). Frameworks therefore fuse the activation into the matmul's epilogue or into a single elementwise kernel with the gating multiply (torch.compile, Triton, or a hand-written SwiGLU kernel; gpu6). Fused, the erf or exp is free; unfused, GELU and SwiGLU are visibly slower than ReLU. The backward pass also needs the activation's input (or output) saved (dl1), which is one reason activation-function choice shows up in the memory arithmetic of gpu3: a SwiGLU block saves the gate branch, the up branch and their product, so its saved activations are larger than a ReLU block's, and selective recomputation (gpu9) often recomputes exactly these cheap elementwise tensors.

Outliers and quantisation

Large transformers develop a few hidden channels with activation magnitudes far larger than the rest; Dettmers et al. (LLM.int8(), 2022) found systematic outlier features emerging at around 6.7B parameters that break naive 8-bit activation quantisation, motivating mixed-precision decomposition and, in SmoothQuant, migrating the difficulty from activations to weights with a per-channel scale. The multiplicative gate of GLU-style FFNs is a natural place for extreme values because a large gate times a large up value gives a very large product. Understanding that the activation choice shapes the distribution of intermediate values, not just their function, is what connects this topic to quantisation (gpu4).

Softmax details that bite

Softmax is shift-invariant (adding a constant to every logit changes nothing) but not scale-invariant (multiplying logits by 2 sharpens the distribution). This is why the numerically stable form subtracts the maximum, and why temperature works. If logits grow large, softmax saturates: one probability approaches 1, the rest approach 0, and the Jacobian diag(p) − ppᵀ goes to zero, so gradients vanish — the same saturation as sigmoid. In attention, where softmax is applied to query-key dot products, unchecked growth of those logits causes exactly this; QK-normalisation and logit soft-capping (used in some LLMs, e.g. Gemma 2) bound the scores to prevent it. A related trick on the output side is label smoothing (dl8), which stops the network from driving logits to extremes.

Approximation mismatches

Because "GELU" names two computations (exact erf and tanh approximation) and "Swish" names a family (x·σ(βx), where SiLU is β = 1), a model can silently use a different variant in training and serving. The per-element difference between the two GELUs is under 5×10⁻⁴, tiny for one layer but not zero after dozens of layers, and it is exactly the kind of small discrepancy that makes a ported model score a fraction of a point lower or diverge from a reference in a layer-by-layer comparison. The remedy is to pin the variant in the configuration and test numerical equivalence on fixed inputs whenever weights cross frameworks.

The public case: Shazeer's controlled comparison and what followed

By 2019 the transformer's feed-forward block still used ReLU (as in the original 2017 paper and in T5) or GELU (BERT, GPT-2). In February 2020 Noam Shazeer (Google) published "GLU Variants Improve Transformer" (arXiv:2002.05202), a four-page test of one question: does replacing the first linear layer and activation of the FFN with a gated unit help? He used the T5 base model (12 encoder and 12 decoder layers, d_model = 768, FFN width 3,072), the C4 text corpus and the span-filling pre-training objective, and kept parameters and compute equal by shrinking the hidden width of gated variants to 2,048 (that is, 3,072 × 2/3). Every model was trained for 524,288 steps with the same settings (a batch of 128 examples, no dropout in pre-training). Table 1 reports held-out log-perplexity (lower is better):

FFN variant65,536 steps524,288 steps
ReLU (baseline)1.9971.677
GELU1.9831.679
Swish1.9941.683
GLU (sigmoid gate)1.9821.663
Bilinear (no activation)1.9601.648
ReGLU1.9531.645
SwiGLU1.9441.636
GEGLU1.9421.633

Read the table for what it does and does not show. Pointwise activations barely differ (GELU and Swish are within noise of ReLU at 524k steps: 1.679 and 1.683 versus 1.677), so "smooth beats ReLU" is not supported here. Every gated variant beats every pointwise one — including the bilinear layer with no activation — and the best gap, 1.633 versus 1.677, is 0.044 log-perplexity. The paper measured run-to-run standard deviations of 0.003–0.010 (four repeats of the 65,536-step runs), so the gated improvement is many times the noise. Fine-tuning results on GLUE, SuperGLUE and SQuAD were noisier, but the gated variants scored best on most tasks. The paper's conclusion is the quote from section 7: no explanation, just results — which is honest, and the right register for an interview.

Adoption followed: PaLM (Google, 2022) used SwiGLU "because they have been shown to significantly increase quality compared to standard ReLU, GeLU, or Swish activations", noting that it needs three matrix multiplications instead of two; LLaMA (Meta, 2023) replaced ReLU with SwiGLU and set the hidden width to 2/3·4d; Llama 3 lists SwiGLU with FFN widths of 14,336, 28,672 and 53,248 for its 8B, 70B and 405B models; Gemma uses the GeGLU variant. Earlier work stayed with GELU: BERT states that it uses GELU "rather than the standard ReLU, following OpenAI GPT".

A port-mismatch story. When Gemma was released in February 2024, a community pull request to the Hugging Face transformers library, "Gemma bug fixes — Approx GELU, Layernorms, Sqrt(hd)" (#29402), listed differences between the library's implementation and the model as trained: the activation should be the tanh-approximate GELU (gelu_pytorch_tanh), not the exact erf form the config's "gelu" resolved to; the layer norm should be computed in float32; and the embedding scale sqrt(hidden size) needed care. The library's Gemma implementation was subsequently changed to use the approximate GELU through a separate hidden_activation setting. The lesson is not that anyone erred grossly; it is that a per-element difference of 10⁻⁴ in an activation is invisible in a unit test and visible as a small quality drop, so activation variants belong in the checkpoint's configuration and in a layer-by-layer equivalence test.

Monitoring activations in a real run

Cheap statistics per layer, logged every few hundred steps, catch most activation problems: the fraction of exactly-zero outputs (ReLU layers: roughly 50% at initialisation is normal; a climbing fraction or units silent on a whole batch means dead units), the mean and standard deviation of activations (steady across depth if initialisation is right; shrinking or exploding by layer means a scale problem), and for saturating activations the fraction of inputs with |z| > 4 (sigmoid/tanh gates in recurrent networks: a high fraction means the gate is stuck open or closed). PyTorch forward hooks (register_forward_hook) make this a dozen lines. Compare against the gradient-norm-per-layer plot (dl3): dead or saturated units show up as layers whose gradient norm is far below its neighbours'.

Failure modes and their symptoms

A large silent fraction of dead ReLUs after an aggressive first few steps: loss plateaus higher than a peer run, and the activation-zero fraction is high. Fix with warmup, lower peak learning rate, and check bias initialisation (a large positive constant bias can also start many units dead in a badly scaled layer).

NaN in softmax or a custom sigmoid gate at low precision: exp overflow. Float16 overflows at inputs above about 11 for exp (its maximum finite value is 65,504) and float32 above about 88; use the fused, max-subtracted implementations and keep activations that involve exponentials or reductions in float32 while matmuls run in bfloat16 (gpu4).

Slow steps caused by an unfused activation. A profile (gpu11) that shows many small elementwise kernels around each matmul — GELU, the gate multiply, dropout — means the activation is memory-bound and not fused; torch.compile or a fused SwiGLU kernel typically removes it.

Exploding activations in gated FFNs. The product of two unbounded branches can produce rare huge values, seen as loss spikes or as outlier channels that wreck int8 quantisation. Mitigations in practice are a smaller learning rate or longer warmup, weight decay, normalisation before the FFN (dl4), and outlier-aware quantisation.

A wrong output activation. Applying softmax and then a loss that itself applies softmax (double softmax) makes the model train slowly and plateau at poor accuracy — logits are compressed to (0, 1) before the loss sees them. The rule is one activation, applied where the loss expects it; use the fused with-logits losses and feed them raw scores.
myths: ReLU won because it is a better function approximator than sigmoid.

Sigmoid networks can represent the same functions. ReLU won because it is easier to optimise: its slope is exactly 1 for positive inputs, so gradients pass through many layers without shrinking, and it is cheap and produces sparse activations. The win is about training dynamics, not about what the network can in principle express.
Dead ReLUs are a rare, minor annoyance.

A ReLU unit whose input is negative for every training example receives exactly zero gradient and can never recover. With a learning rate that is too high, or a large negative bias, a substantial fraction of a layer (in the lab, over 40% at a learning rate of 3) can die silently in the first few steps. Loss still decreases — the network just has less capacity than you paid for — so you only see it if you log the fraction of zero activations.
GELU, SiLU and SwiGLU are used because they are smooth, and smoothness is what matters.

Smoothness (a non-zero gradient for small negative inputs) probably helps a little, but the strongest evidence is empirical: in Shazeer's controlled comparison, swapping ReLU for GELU or Swish barely moved held-out perplexity, while gated variants lowered it clearly. The gain comes from the multiplicative gate — two projections multiplied together — not from the shape of the curve alone, and the paper offers no theoretical explanation.
Softmax is just another activation you can put in hidden layers.

Softmax couples all the units in a layer: raising one output forces the others down because they must sum to 1. That is exactly what you want for a distribution over classes and wrong for a hidden layer, whose units should be free to activate independently. (Attention uses softmax to build a weighting over positions, which is a different job.)
A more complicated activation is more expensive to run.

Activation functions cost almost nothing next to the matrix multiplies around them. On a GPU an elementwise GELU or SiLU is limited by memory traffic, not arithmetic, and compilers fuse it into the neighbouring matmul so the extra exp or erf is hidden. The real cost of SwiGLU is a third weight matrix in the feed-forward block, and the standard fix is to shrink the hidden width to about 2/3 so total parameters and FLOPs match.
The choice of activation function can be made independently of initialisation.

They are coupled. A ReLU zeroes about half its inputs, halving the signal's second moment, so weights need variance 2/fan_in (He initialisation) to keep signal size steady; with the tanh-oriented 1/fan_in rule the signal decays by a factor of about 2 per layer. In a quick experiment, ten ReLU layers with He initialisation kept the root-mean-square activation at 0.95, while the 1/fan_in rule left 0.03.
lab:
Goal: tabulate GELU and SiLU by hand-written formulas, train the same small network with six different activations on data no linear model can fit, and watch dead ReLU units appear as the learning rate rises. NumPy only, Python 3.12; runs in under a minute. The network is 2 → 16 → 16 → 1 with hand-written backprop (exactly the loop of dl1) so you see how f′(z) enters the backward pass.

import numpy as np
from math import erf, sqrt

# ---- activation functions and their derivatives (all vectorised)
erf_v = np.vectorize(erf)
Phi = lambda z: 0.5 * (1 + erf_v(z / sqrt(2)))
phi = lambda z: np.exp(-z ** 2 / 2) / sqrt(2 * np.pi)
sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
ACTS = {
    "linear":  (lambda z: z,                lambda z: np.ones_like(z)),
    "sigmoid": (sig,                        lambda z: sig(z) * (1 - sig(z))),
    "tanh":    (np.tanh,                    lambda z: 1 - np.tanh(z) ** 2),
    "relu":    (lambda z: np.maximum(z, 0), lambda z: (z > 0).astype(float)),
    "gelu":    (lambda z: z * Phi(z),       lambda z: Phi(z) + z * phi(z)),
    "silu":    (lambda z: z * sig(z),       lambda z: sig(z) * (1 + z * (1 - sig(z)))),
}

print("z      gelu    silu   sigmoid'   tanh'")
for z in [-2.0, -0.5, 0.5, 2.0]:
    zz = np.array([z])
    print(f"{z:4}  {ACTS['gelu'][0](zz)[0]:7.3f} {ACTS['silu'][0](zz)[0]:7.3f} {ACTS['sigmoid'][1](zz)[0]:8.3f} {ACTS['tanh'][1](zz)[0]:8.3f}")

# ---- data: two concentric circles (not linearly separable)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 400
ang = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n); rad = np.where(np.arange(n) < n // 2, 1.0, 2.0) + rng.normal(0, 0.1, n)
X = np.c_[rad * np.cos(ang), rad * np.sin(ang)]; y = (np.arange(n) >= n // 2).astype(float)[:, None]

def train(act, lr=0.1, steps=2000, width=16, seed=1):
    f, df = ACTS[act]
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    sizes = [2, width, width, 1]
    W = [r.normal(0, sqrt(2 / a), (a, b)) for a, b in zip(sizes, sizes[1:])]
    b = [np.zeros(k) for k in sizes[1:]]
    for _ in range(steps):
        zs, hs = [], [X]                               # forward: keep pre-activations and activations
        for i in range(3):
            zs.append(hs[-1] @ W[i] + b[i])
            hs.append(f(zs[-1]) if i < 2 else zs[-1])   # last layer is linear (logits)
        p = sig(zs[-1])
        d = (p - y) / n                                # dL/dlogits for sigmoid + binary cross-entropy
        for i in (2, 1, 0):                            # backward
            gW, gb = hs[i].T @ d, d.sum(0)
            if i > 0: d = (d @ W[i].T) * df(zs[i - 1])
            W[i] -= lr * gW; b[i] -= lr * gb
    acc = ((p > 0.5) == (y > 0.5)).mean()
    dead = np.mean([(hs[i + 1].max(0) <= 1e-12).mean() for i in range(2)]) if act == "relu" else float("nan")
    return acc, dead

print("\nactivation   accuracy on circles")
for name in ACTS: print(f"{name:9}    {train(name)[0]:.3f}")

print("\nReLU dead units vs learning rate (fraction of hidden units silent on ALL 400 examples)")
for lr in [0.05, 0.3, 1.0, 3.0]:
    acc, dead = train("relu", lr=lr, steps=300)
    print(f"lr={lr:<5} accuracy {acc:.3f}   dead {dead:.2f}")

# ---- parameter count: standard FFN vs SwiGLU with the 2/3 rule
d = 4096; print("\nstandard FFN 4d:", 2 * d * 4 * d, " SwiGLU 8/3 d:", 3 * d * round(8 * d / 3))

What to look for.

  1. The value table reproduces the numbers in the lesson: GELU(−2) = −0.046, SiLU(−2) = −0.238, sigmoid′(±2) = 0.105, tanh′(±0.5) = 0.786.
  2. The accuracy table. The two rings of points cannot be separated by a line, so linear stays near chance (about 0.53) however long it trains — a network with no non-linearity is one linear layer. Tanh, ReLU, GELU and SiLU all reach 1.000 in 2,000 full-batch steps. Sigmoid is clearly behind (about 0.74 in the reference run): its small, saturating slopes and non-zero-centred outputs make it the slowest learner. Set steps=20000 for sigmoid to see it eventually get there.
  3. The dead-unit table. After 300 steps, the fraction of hidden ReLU units that output exactly zero for all 400 examples is about 3–6% at learning rates 0.05–1 and about 41% at 3.0. The network still fits the training data — dead units are silent, not fatal — which is why you must measure them.
  4. The parameter count line confirms the 2/3 rule: the two-matrix FFN and the three-matrix SwiGLU at width 8d/3 hold 134.2 million weights each at d = 4,096.

Try next. Add a swiglu block (two first-layer matrices and a product) and check its gradient with the finite-difference test from dl1; initialise the ReLU network with variance 1/n instead of 2/n and compare the first-layer gradient norms with a deeper stack of layers.
recap: Without a non-linearity a stack of layers is one matrix multiplication, so depth adds nothing; the activation function is what lets a network represent curves, corners and functions like XOR that no linear map can.

Sigmoid and tanh saturate: their slopes fall to nearly zero for large inputs and, for sigmoid, never exceed 0.25, so backprop through many such layers shrinks gradients by a constant factor per layer (about 10⁻⁶ after ten layers at best for sigmoid).

ReLU = max(0, z) has slope exactly 1 on the positive side, costs one comparison, and yields sparse activations, which is why it made deep networks trainable; AlexNet reached 25% training error on CIFAR-10 six times faster with ReLU than with tanh.

A ReLU unit whose input is negative for every example has zero gradient forever (a dead unit); high learning rates and large negative biases cause it, Leaky ReLU, PReLU or smoother activations avoid it, and the fraction of zero activations per layer is the diagnostic.
GELU = z·Φ(z) and SiLU = z·σ(z) are smooth ReLU-like curves with a small negative dip; they replaced ReLU in BERT, GPT-style models and many vision networks.

A gated linear unit multiplies two linear projections, one passed through an activation: SwiGLU(x) = SiLU(xW) ⊙ xV; it needs three weight matrices instead of two, so the hidden width is scaled by 2/3 to keep the parameter count the same.

In Shazeer's T5 experiments, gated variants (GEGLU 1.942, SwiGLU 1.944) beat ReLU (1.997) in held-out log-perplexity at equal parameters and compute, and PaLM, LLaMA and Llama 3 adopted SwiGLU while Gemma uses GeGLU.

Output activations are paired with losses — linear with MSE, sigmoid with binary cross-entropy, softmax with categorical cross-entropy — and in each fused pairing the gradient with respect to the logits is simply p − y.

Activation and initialisation interact: He initialisation (variance 2/fan_in) compensates for ReLU zeroing half the signal, and the wrong pairing makes activations shrink or grow exponentially with depth.

drill:
Work it out

Evaluate ReLU, GELU and SiLU at z = −2, −0.5, 0.5, 2 (use Φ(−2) = 0.02275, Φ(−0.5) = 0.3085, Φ(0.5) = 0.6915, Φ(2) = 0.97725, and σ(−2) = 0.1192, σ(−0.5) = 0.3775, σ(0.5) = 0.6225, σ(2) = 0.8808). Then explain precisely how a ReLU unit dies and why a GELU unit cannot die in the same way.

Answer
zReLUGELU = z·Φ(z)SiLU = z·σ(z)
−20−2 × 0.02275 = −0.046−2 × 0.1192 = −0.238
−0.50−0.5 × 0.3085 = −0.154−0.5 × 0.3775 = −0.189
0.50.50.5 × 0.6915 = 0.3460.5 × 0.6225 = 0.311
222 × 0.97725 = 1.9542 × 0.8808 = 1.762

How a ReLU dies. Its slope is exactly 0 for z < 0. If a large update pushes a unit's bias so negative that z < 0 for every example in the data, the unit outputs 0 and every gradient through it — with respect to its input weights and its own bias — is exactly 0. Gradient descent only moves parameters in response to gradients, so nothing can move it back: it is permanently dead, and with an oversized learning rate this can silently take out a large share of a layer.

Why GELU cannot die this way. Its slope is non-zero for moderate negative inputs (about −0.085 at z = −2 and −0.083 at z = −1), so a gradient still reaches a unit sitting in the negative region, and a suitable update can bring it back. Very negative inputs (below about −4) do give a near-zero slope, so GELU can become practically inactive; it just does not have the exact, permanent zero that ReLU does. The trade-off is cost: GELU needs an erf or tanh and SiLU an exp, which is invisible when fused into a matmul but real when it is not.

Size it up

A team wants to swap the ReLU FFN of a 32-layer model (d = 4,096, FFN width 16,384) for SwiGLU without changing the parameter count. What hidden width do they choose, and how many FFN parameters does the whole model hold before and after?

Answer

Standard FFN per layer: 2 × 4,096 × 16,384 = 134,217,728 weights. SwiGLU has three matrices, so 3 × 4,096 × h = 134,217,728 gives h = 10,922.7. Round to a multiple of 256 for tensor-core friendliness: h = 10,752 or 11,008 (LLaMA's choice; 3 × 4,096 × 11,008 = 135,266,304, +0.8%). Over 32 layers: 4.29 billion FFN weights before (134.2M × 32), 4.33 billion with h = 11,008. Compute per token follows the same count (each weight is one multiply-add, 2 FLOPs, in the forward pass), so the swap is neutral in parameters and FLOPs; what changes is that three smaller matmuls run instead of two larger ones, and an extra elementwise gate multiply that should be fused. If instead they keep h = 16,384, the FFN grows by 50% (201M weights per layer) — a legitimate choice, but then any quality gain is confounded with the extra parameters, which is what the 2/3 rule avoids.
qa: E
Why do neural networks need activation functions?

Each layer without an activation is a matrix multiplication, and a product of matrices is another matrix, so a 50-layer linear network is no more expressive than one linear layer — it can only draw straight-line boundaries. The activation bends the function so each layer adds something new. A concrete case is XOR: no linear map can separate it, but two ReLU units can.
E
Why is ReLU the default in hidden layers of CNNs and MLPs?

Its slope is exactly 1 for positive inputs and 0 for negative ones, so gradients pass through unchanged instead of shrinking at every layer like sigmoid's (at most 0.25). It is also nearly free to compute (a comparison), produces sparse activations, and needs no exponentials. AlexNet reported reaching 25% training error on CIFAR-10 six times faster with ReLU than with tanh.
E
Why is softmax not used as a hidden-layer activation?

It couples all units in the layer through a normalisation, forcing them to compete for a fixed budget of 1. That is right for a distribution over classes and wrong for intermediate features, which should be free to be active together. Softmax belongs on the output, paired with cross-entropy.
E
What is a dead ReLU and how do you detect one?

A unit whose pre-activation is negative for every input outputs 0 and has slope 0, so no gradient reaches its weights and it never recovers. Log the fraction of exactly-zero activations per layer over a batch; a large and growing fraction (well above the usual ~50%) or units silent on the whole batch is the signature. Common causes are a learning rate that is too high or a large negative bias; remedies are lower learning rate, warmup, Leaky ReLU/GELU, and He initialisation.
M
Why do sigmoid and tanh cause vanishing gradients?

Both saturate: for large |z| their slope is almost zero, and sigmoid's slope never exceeds 0.25 (at z = 0). Backprop multiplies one such slope per layer, so ten sigmoid layers scale the gradient by at most 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁶, and tanh at |z| = 1 (slope 0.42) by about 2×10⁻⁴. Early layers then receive almost no learning signal. Sigmoid is also not zero-centred, which makes downstream weight updates share a sign and zig-zag.

Follow-up: Does ReLU solve vanishing gradients completely? — It removes the per-layer shrinkage on active paths, but depth still needs sensible initialisation, normalisation and residual connections (dl3).
M
What is GELU and why do transformers use it instead of ReLU?

GELU(z) = z·Φ(z), where Φ is the standard normal CDF, so it scales the input by the probability that a standard normal variable is below it: a smooth gate instead of ReLU's hard threshold. It is close to ReLU for large |z| but is smooth at 0 and has a small negative dip (minimum ≈ −0.17 near z = −0.75). BERT and GPT-2 adopted it because it trained a little better in practice; the evidence is empirical rather than a proof.

Follow-up: How is it computed in practice? — Either exactly with erf, or with the tanh approximation 0.5z(1 + tanh(√(2/π)(z + 0.044715z³))), whose error is under 5×10⁻⁴; make sure the framework and checkpoint agree on which one.
M
What is SwiGLU and why does it use a smaller hidden dimension?

SwiGLU(x) = SiLU(xW) ⊙ (xV): two parallel linear projections, one passed through SiLU as a gate, multiplied elementwise, then projected back with W₂. That is three weight matrices instead of the two of a standard FFN, so with the usual 4d hidden width it would have 1.5× the parameters. Scaling the hidden width by 2/3 (≈ 8d/3) restores 2·d·4d = 3·d·(8d/3) = 8d² parameters and FLOPs, which keeps comparisons fair. LLaMA states it uses 2/3·4d; implementations round to a hardware-friendly multiple, giving 11,008 for d = 4,096.

Follow-up: Why does gating help? — Multiplying two projections gives the layer input-dependent, multiplicative interactions a pointwise activation cannot express; Shazeer reports the gain empirically and offers no theory.
M
Pair each output activation with a loss for regression, binary, multi-class and multi-label tasks.

Regression: linear output with MSE or Huber. Binary: sigmoid with binary cross-entropy. Multi-class (one label): softmax with categorical cross-entropy. Multi-label (several labels can be true): independent sigmoids with binary cross-entropy per label. Use the fused 'with logits' loss functions, which apply log-sum-exp internally for stability, and the gradient with respect to the logits is p − y in each classification case.
M
How do activation choice and initialisation interact?

Initialisation is chosen so that the signal's variance stays constant layer to layer. ReLU zeroes half of its inputs, halving the second moment, so weights need variance 2/fan_in (He). Tanh and sigmoid near zero are roughly linear with slope 1 (tanh) or 0.25 (sigmoid) and are matched by Xavier's 2/(fan_in + fan_out). Using the wrong scale makes activations and gradients shrink or grow exponentially with depth: in a 10-layer, width-1000 test, He init kept RMS at 0.95 while 1/fan_in left 0.03.
H
Why do ReLU networks work so well despite the function being piecewise linear?

A ReLU network computes a piecewise-linear function, but the number of distinct linear pieces can grow exponentially with depth, so it can approximate smooth functions closely. Each unit is a hyperplane fold; composing layers folds space repeatedly. Piecewise linearity also keeps gradients simple: on any region the network is exactly linear, the slope is a product of 0/1 gates and weights, and there is no saturation. The cost is that the second derivative is zero almost everywhere and units can die.
H
Design the feed-forward block of a new 7B decoder-only LLM. Which activation, what hidden size, what parameter count?

Use a gated unit, SwiGLU by default (GeGLU is equivalent in practice), with no biases. With d = 4,096, choose the hidden width near 8d/3 ≈ 10,923 and round to a multiple of 256 for tensor-core efficiency, giving 11,008 as LLaMA-7B does. The block has 3 × 4,096 × 11,008 ≈ 135M parameters per layer, against 134M for a ReLU/GELU FFN with 4d, so the total stays about 6.7B for 32 layers. If the budget allows a bigger FFN (Llama 3 8B uses 14,336 ≈ 3.5d) that is a separate scaling choice, not a property of the activation.

Follow-up: What would make you use squared ReLU instead? — A goal of activation sparsity for cheaper inference, or hardware where the extra gate matmul is not worth it; Nemotron-4 15B uses squared ReLU.
H
A model ported between frameworks gives slightly different outputs even though the weights match. Activation-related suspects?

Check the exact activation: GELU exact (erf) versus tanh approximation differ by up to about 5×10⁻⁴ per element, enough to shift logits after many layers. Gemma, for example, was trained with the tanh approximation, and an early Hugging Face port used the exact form until it was fixed. Also check SiLU versus Swish with β ≠ 1, the order of the gate and up projections in a SwiGLU checkpoint, whether the activation runs in float32 or bfloat16, and the epsilon or clamping used in softmax and log-sum-exp. Compare layer by layer against a reference on a fixed input to locate the first divergence.
H
Where do activation functions cause numerical trouble in low-precision training?

Anything with an exponential: softmax with logits above about 88 overflows float32, and above about 11 overflows float16's e^z range (max 65,504), so implementations subtract the maximum first. Sigmoid and softplus need stable forms. SwiGLU multiplies two projections, which can create rare very large activation outliers that make int8 activation quantisation hard, motivating outlier-aware schemes such as LLM.int8() and SmoothQuant. Doing the activation and reductions in float32 while keeping matmuls in bf16 is the usual mitigation.

sum: Why the gradient at the first layer is a product of one factor per layer and so shrinks or grows exponentially with depth, how initialisation, normalisation, residual connections, gating and clipping each fix a different part of the problem, and how to see it in a real run.
prereq: dl1
Backprop multiplies the incoming gradient by each layer's local Jacobian; the gradient at layer 1 is a product of one factor per layer above it.
dl2
Sigmoid and tanh have slopes below 1 (sigmoid at most 0.25) and saturate; ReLU has slope exactly 1 on active units and needs He initialisation.
ml4
Gradient descent steps by the learning rate times the gradient, so the gradient's size directly sets how far weights move, and exploding gradients cause divergence.
why:
An engineer takes a network that works at 8 layers and, reasonably, tries 40. The training loss now sits stubbornly at its starting value. Printing the size of the weight changes shows a striking pattern: the last few layers are updating normally, and the first ten layers are moving by a millionth of what they should — or not at all. In another team, the same kind of change gives the opposite symptom: the loss falls nicely for two hundred steps and then leaps to NaN, with the weights suddenly enormous. Same architectural move, two opposite failures, and both come from the same one-line piece of arithmetic.

The arithmetic is the chain rule (dl1): the gradient that reaches the first layer is the gradient at the loss multiplied by one factor for every layer in between. Multiply forty numbers that are each slightly below 1 and the result is tiny; multiply forty numbers slightly above 1 and it is huge. Depth turns a small per-layer bias into an exponential one. For decades this limited neural networks to a handful of layers: it is why sigmoid networks were hard to train, why recurrent networks could not remember what happened fifty steps ago, and why "deeper" was for years a way of making models worse.

The story has a surprising twist that makes this topic a favourite of interviewers. The deep-network breakthroughs of 2010–2015 — variance-preserving initialisation, normalisation layers, and above all residual connections — are usually credited with "curing vanishing gradients". But the ResNet authors themselves, having trained plain 34-layer networks with normalisation in which they checked that gradients were healthy, still saw those networks train worse than 18-layer ones. The truth is more subtle than the folk story, and being able to say why marks the difference between knowing the slogan and understanding the mechanism.

This lesson starts from the smallest possible model, a chain of scalar multiplications with real numbers, and builds up to matrices, random initialisation and the variance arguments behind Xavier and He initialisation. We then measure a 30-layer network by hand-written backprop to see the effect directly, study each of the fixes (initialisation, normalisation, residual connections, gates, clipping) for what it changes and what it does not, and finish with how loss spikes are handled in real large-model training. The public case is the ResNet paper, checked against its own numbers.
primer:
The telephone game

Remember the game where a message is whispered down a line of people. If each person repeats only half of what they heard, the message from the far end is unrecognisable — nothing is left. If each person exaggerates by half, a small rumour becomes a grotesque story. A neural network's error signal travelling from the loss back to the first layer is that message, and each layer is one person in the line, scaling what it receives by some factor. Backprop multiplies those factors together, so what reaches the first layer is the original signal times the product of all the factors.

The numbers make it concrete. Thirty factors of 0.5 multiply to 0.5³⁰ ≈ 9×10⁻¹⁰: about a billionth. Thirty factors of 1.5 multiply to 1.5³⁰ ≈ 191,751: nearly two hundred thousand. Call the typical per-layer factor the gain. A gain of exactly 1 preserves the signal; anything else, applied at every layer, is exponential in depth. The chart shows how quickly it gets out of hand: over 100 layers, a gain of 0.8 loses ten orders of magnitude and a gain of 1.2 gains eight.

The analogy breaks in one useful place: the people in a real line are all the same, but a network's layers are matrices, which scale different directions by different amounts. A layer can shrink the signal along one direction and stretch it along another, and the product of many such layers stretches some directions enormously while crushing others. We will need that for the full picture, but the scalar case already contains the essential idea.

Two failures, two sets of symptoms

  • Vanishing gradients: the loss stalls early; gradient norms in early layers are orders of magnitude below those in late layers; early-layer weights barely change. The network is effectively a shallow network sitting on top of layers that stayed random.
  • Exploding gradients: the loss spikes or turns NaN/inf; a step is far too large and throws the weights somewhere terrible; the global gradient norm shoots up before the loss does.

The fixes, in one line each

  • Better activations (ReLU family) remove the shrinking slope factor (dl2).
  • Careful initialisation starts each layer's gain at about 1 (Xavier, He).
  • Normalisation layers re-centre and re-scale activations at every layer, so the scale cannot drift (dl4).
  • Residual (skip) connections: each block computes x + f(x), so the gradient always has a direct path.
  • Gates (LSTM, GRU) give recurrent networks the same kind of additive path across time (dl7).
  • Gradient clipping caps the size of any single gradient, protecting against explosion but not vanishing.

The residual trick in one line: the derivative of x + f(x) with respect to x is 1 + f′(x). Even if f′ is tiny, the 1 remains, so gradients reach early layers through the chain of "+x" paths undiminished. The rest of the lesson explains each fix well enough to say what it changes and where it stops helping.
body:
1. The scalar chain: real numbers

Take the simplest possible deep network: one neuron per layer, each computing h_l = f(w·h_{l−1}) with the same weight w. By the chain rule (dl1), the derivative of the last layer's output with respect to the input is the product of one factor w·f′(z_l) per layer — the gain of that layer. If every gain is the same number g, then after L layers the gradient is scaled by g^L:

gain gL = 10L = 30L = 100
0.50.0019.3×10⁻¹⁰7.9×10⁻³¹
0.90.350.0422.7×10⁻⁵

Notice how narrow the survivable band is: a gain 10% off in either direction is harmless at 10 layers and ruinous at 100. Now run an actual tanh chain, h_l = tanh(w·h_{l−1}) starting from h₀ = 0.5, for 10 layers and compute the true end-to-end derivative dh₁₀/dh₀ as the product of w(1 − h_l²):

weight wfinal h₁₀dh₁₀/dh₀what happened
0.50.00059×10⁻⁴weight gain 0.5 per layer: vanishes
1.00.300.22near the critical gain, but tanh's slope still trims it
1.50.866×10⁻⁴units drift into the flat region: vanishes
2.50.9867×10⁻¹¹units saturated at ≈ 1: slope ≈ 0.03, vanishes

The bottom row is the instructive one. A weight of 2.5 looks like it should amplify, and per-layer the weight does; but in a saturating network larger weights drive every unit into a flat region, where the slope factor is tiny, and the gradient vanishes far more severely than with a small weight. The total gain is weight × slope, not weight alone. This is why "exploding gradient means large weights" is only half true: in sigmoid and tanh networks the failure is mostly on the vanishing side, and real explosions need units that stay responsive, which is what ReLU (slope exactly 1 when active) and recurrent networks provide.

2. From scalars to layers: Jacobians and singular values

Real layers map vectors to vectors, and the "factor" for a layer is its Jacobian J, the matrix of partial derivatives of the layer's outputs with respect to its inputs (dl1). The backward pass multiplies the gradient vector by one Jacobian per layer, and what matters at each step is how much that matrix stretches the vector's length. A matrix's stretching is described by its singular values: the largest is the most it can stretch any vector, the smallest the least. A worked case with a 2×2 layer W = [[0.6, 0.2], [−0.2, 0.6]] (a rotation combined with a shrink): both singular values equal √(0.6² + 0.2²) = 0.632. Push a gradient (1, 0) back through the layer repeatedly using Wᵀ: after one layer it is (0.6, 0.2) with length 0.632; after two, (0.32, 0.24), length 0.400; after three, (0.144, 0.208), length 0.253. The length is multiplied by 0.632 each time — after ten such layers, 0.01. The gradient is not merely rotating; it is vanishing, because every direction is shrunk.

For a general matrix the picture is richer: some directions grow while others shrink, and a product of many matrices can stretch a few directions to enormous size while crushing the rest. To have every direction preserved through depth, all singular values of the product must stay near 1 — the condition called dynamical isometry (deep section). For this lesson, the useful shortcut is the behaviour of random matrices, which is what an initialised network has.

Take a layer with n inputs whose weights are independent random numbers of variance σ². Feed it a vector of length 1; the output is n·(something) sums of random terms, and its expected squared length is n·σ², so its length is about σ√n. The gain of a random layer is σ√n, and it equals 1 when σ² = 1/n. An experiment confirms the prediction: 30 random 100×100 layers with σ√n = 0.8, 1.0 and 1.2 shrank a unit-length vector to 0.001, 0.56 and 134 (prediction 0.8³⁰ = 0.0012, 1.0³⁰ = 1, 1.2³⁰ = 237, close given the randomness). There is a critical scale, σ² = 1/n, and being 20% off it on either side is fatal at depth 30.

3. Forward signals and backward gradients follow the same rule

The same product structure governs the forward pass: the size of the activations at layer l is the input's size times the product of gains of the layers below. And the backward gradient is the loss gradient times the product of gains of the layers above (transposed). So a badly scaled initialisation damages both at once: too small, and activations shrink toward zero going up while gradients shrink toward zero going down; too large, and both explode. This is why the classic fixes are stated as "keep the variance of activations and of gradients constant across layers".

Glorot & Bengio (2010) worked out the conditions for a linear-ish layer with n_in inputs and n_out outputs. Forward variance stays constant if n_in·Var(w) = 1; backward variance stays constant if n_out·Var(w) = 1. When n_in ≠ n_out both cannot hold, so they compromise: Xavier (Glorot) initialisation, Var(w) = 2/(n_in + n_out). This assumes the activation is approximately the identity near zero with slope 1, as tanh is. For ReLU it is wrong, by a factor of two, for the reason from dl2: ReLU outputs zero for negative inputs, so the mean square of its output is half that of its input. Each layer therefore loses half the second moment, a gain of √½ ≈ 0.71 in length. He initialisation (He et al., 2015), Var(w) = 2/n_in, doubles the weight variance to compensate. With width n = 100, Xavier gives σ = 0.1 (1/√n), He gives σ = 0.141 (√(2/n)); with n = 1,000 the values are 0.032 and 0.045.

4. Measuring it: a 30-layer network

To see all of this at once, the lab builds a plain 30-layer, width-100 network with hand-written backprop and measures the size of the gradient reaching every layer's input relative to the top layer. Results (the lab prints exactly these):

Setupgradient at layer 1 ÷ at layer 30Verdict
sigmoid, N(0, 0.1²)5×10⁻¹⁹vanishes completely
tanh, σ = 0.05 (too small)1×10⁻⁹vanishes (gain ≈ 0.5)
tanh, Xavier σ = 1/√n0.14healthy (mild saturation loss)
tanh, σ = 0.25 (too big)1×10³explodes
ReLU, σ = 1/√n (Xavier-like)3×10⁻⁴vanishes (lost ½ per layer)
ReLU, He σ = √(2/n)6healthy
ReLU, σ = 2/√n (too big)1×10⁵explodes
ReLU, He + residual, unscaled8×10⁶explodes (branches add up)
ReLU, He/√L + residual17healthy

A subtlety the lab exposes: the gradient of a layer's weights is (layer input)ᵀ × (backward signal) (dl1, section 5), and with a too-small init both factors shrink in opposite directions along depth — inputs shrink going up while the backward signal shrinks going down — so the product can look nearly constant across layers, only tiny in absolute terms (about 10⁻¹⁰ for the too-small tanh network). Comparing weight-gradient norms across layers can therefore hide a scale problem; compare the backward signal and the activations too.

5. Fix 1: initialisation

  • Xavier/Glorot, Var(w) = 2/(n_in + n_out): for tanh, sigmoid, linear layers.
  • He/Kaiming, Var(w) = 2/n_in: for ReLU and its relatives.
  • Orthogonal: all singular values exactly 1, so lengths are preserved exactly; used for recurrent weights and in theory of very deep networks.
  • Biases to zero, usually, and for residual networks the last layer of each residual branch to zero or a small value, so every block starts as the identity.
  • Transformers: normal with standard deviation 0.02 for most weights, and the output projection of each residual branch scaled by about 1/√N, where N is the number of residual layers, as in GPT-2 — for 96 residual layers (48 blocks with two branches each), 1/√96 ≈ 0.10.

Initialisation only guarantees a good start. Once training moves the weights, the gains drift, and nothing keeps them in the right range. That is why normalisation exists.

6. Fix 2: normalisation layers

A normalisation layer (dl4 covers them properly) re-centres and re-scales its inputs so that they have a fixed mean and variance at every forward pass — for example, LayerNorm makes each token's vector have zero mean and unit variance across its features, and RMSNorm just divides by the root-mean-square. Whatever the previous layer's weights have drifted to, the scale entering the next layer is reset. Two things follow for gradients: the forward activations are kept in a healthy range (so saturation and blow-up are avoided), and the backward pass through a normaliser is automatically adjusted by the inverse of that scale, so gradient sizes do not depend on the weight scale of the layer beneath it. This is the reason BatchNorm allowed larger learning rates and made init less critical. A caution from the ResNet story below: normalisation alone did not fully solve depth.

7. Fix 3: residual connections

A residual block computes x_{l+1} = x_l + F_l(x_l), where F is a small stack of layers. Its Jacobian is I + J_F: the identity plus whatever F contributes. Backward, the gradient arriving at x_{l+1} splits: one copy goes straight through the "+" with gain exactly 1, the other goes through F and is multiplied by J_F. At x_l the two are added: ∂L/∂x_l = ∂L/∂x_{l+1} · (I + J_F). Unroll L blocks and the product (I + J_L)…(I + J_1) expands into a sum: the identity term (a path of gain 1 through every skip), plus each J_i alone (a path through one branch), plus pairs, triples, and so on — 2^L paths of many lengths.

Veit et al. (2016) read this expansion as an ensemble of paths of different lengths and measured how much of the gradient each path length carries. Their finding: in a 110-layer ResNet, most of the gradient comes from paths only 10–34 layers deep; the very long paths, which would suffer vanishing, contribute almost nothing. Deleting a single block from a trained ResNet at test time hurts modestly, whereas deleting one layer from a plain VGG-style network is catastrophic — so residual networks do not depend on every layer in series. Residual connections do not remove the product problem; they add short paths that bypass it.

Residual sums can still explode. A residual stream adds each branch's output: if the branches have output variance v and are roughly independent, the variance after L blocks grows like 1 + L·v — for v = 1 and L = 100 the standard deviation is ≈ 10, and the gradient similarly accumulates. The lab shows it: a 30-layer residual net with He-initialised branches had a first-layer gradient 8 million times that of the last layer. The fixes are to scale the branch initialisation by about 1/√L (variance L·(v/L) = v, so the total stays constant; the lab's scaled version gives 17), to zero-initialise each branch's final layer, or to add a learnable scalar per branch (ReZero, LayerScale), and to use normalisation in the branch (pre-norm) so the stream's scale does not feed back into the branch's input.

What the ResNet paper actually claimed. The paper asks a sharper question than "do gradients vanish?": if a shallow network can do a job, a deeper one could in principle copy it and make the extra layers identity, so it should never be worse on the training set. Empirically it was: on ImageNet the plain 34-layer network had higher training error than the plain 18-layer one, even though it used batch normalisation. The authors argue "this optimization difficulty is unlikely to be caused by vanishing gradients": with BN forward signals have non-zero variance, and they "verify that the backward propagated gradients exhibit healthy norms". They called it the degradation problem and proposed learning residuals F(x) = H(x) − x, which makes the identity (F = 0) trivially reachable. The gradient-flow view above (a clean gain-1 path) is one plausible reason it works, but the paper's own claim is about optimisation difficulty in general, and saying so precisely is worth points.

8. Fix 4: gates for sequences

A recurrent network applies the same weights at every time step, so a gradient travelling back T steps is multiplied by the recurrent Jacobian T times, and its size scales like the spectral radius (largest eigenvalue magnitude) of that matrix, times the activation slope, to the power T. A radius below 1 gives vanishing (the network cannot learn dependencies more than a few steps long); above 1, exploding. The LSTM (dl7) rewrites the state update as c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t−1} + i_t ⊙ g_t: an additive update, gated by a forget gate f_t that the network can hold near 1. When f_t ≈ 1 the derivative of c_t with respect to c_{t−1} is about 1, the same identity path as a residual connection but through time. Truncated backpropagation through time, unrolling only the last k steps, limits how long the product can grow.

9. Exploding gradients: clipping

Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio (2013) described why recurrent networks explode with a picture: the loss surface has narrow high-slope "cliffs". Far from a cliff the gradient is modest; at its edge it becomes enormous, and a normal step multiplied by that enormous gradient throws the parameters far across the landscape, undoing progress. The remedy is gradient norm clipping: if the norm of the gradient exceeds a threshold, rescale the gradient to have exactly that norm, keeping its direction.

The mechanics, with numbers. Suppose the gradients of a model, concatenated across all parameters, have components (3, 4, 12). The global norm is √(9 + 16 + 144) = 13. With a threshold of 1.0 every gradient is multiplied by 1/13, giving (0.23, 0.31, 0.92), whose norm is 1 and whose direction is unchanged. If the norm had been 0.7, nothing would happen: the scale factor is min(1, threshold/norm). This is global-norm clipping and it is what torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ does. Clipping each value separately (clip_grad_value_) distorts the direction (a gradient (0.1, 100) would become (0.1, 1), a different direction) and is rarely used.

scaler.scale(loss).backward()                 # mixed precision with fp16: scaled loss
scaler.unscale_(optimizer)                    # bring gradients back to true scale FIRST
gnorm = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
scaler.step(optimizer); scaler.update()       # (with bf16 there is no scaler; just backward + clip + step)
log({"grad_norm": gnorm.item(), "clipped": gnorm.item() > 1.0})

The order matters: clipping scaled gradients would compare a scaled norm with an unscaled threshold. clip_grad_norm_ returns the pre-clip norm, which is the number to log: it is one of the best training-health signals there is. A typical threshold is 1.0 (LLaMA and PaLM both use global-norm clipping at 1.0); pick it from a healthy run's typical norm so that clipping fires rarely, and track the fraction of steps clipped — a rising fraction says training is drifting toward instability.

10. A diagnosis playbook

SymptomLikely causeFirst checks and fixes
