deep:
Dynamical isometry and orthogonal initialisation

The scalar-gain picture hides a matrix subtlety. Even when a random layer's average gain is exactly 1, its singular values are spread over a range (for a square Gaussian matrix, from near 0 up to about 2 times the average). A product of L such matrices has singular values spread over an exponentially wider range: a few directions are stretched enormously and most are crushed. The gradient's average length can be constant while a typical direction still vanishes. Saxe, McClelland and Ganguli (2013) named the desirable state dynamical isometry — all singular values of the network's input–output Jacobian concentrated near 1 — and Pennington, Schoenholz and Ganguli (2017) extended the analysis to non-linear networks. Orthogonal matrices have all singular values exactly 1, so a stack of them preserves lengths; with a suitably scaled activation the property can be kept through a non-linear network. Xiao et al. (2018) used a mean-field analysis and an orthogonal "delta" initialisation to train vanilla convolutional networks with 10,000 layers, without residual connections or normalisation, which demonstrates that depth alone was never the fundamental obstacle. The same line of work identifies an "edge of chaos", the boundary between the regime where perturbations die out (vanishing) and the one where they blow up (exploding), and shows that initialisation should sit at that edge. In practice residual connections and normalisation reach the same goal with far less fuss, but this theory explains why they work and is why orthogonal initialisation persists for recurrent weights.

Pre-norm versus post-norm, and very deep transformers

In the original transformer the layer norm sits after the residual addition (post-norm), so the normaliser is on the main path and every block's output passes through one. At initialisation this makes the gradient near the output layers large relative to the rest, which is why post-norm transformers need a careful learning-rate warmup and are fragile as depth grows. Moving the normaliser inside the branch (pre-norm: x + F(Norm(x))) leaves the residual stream a clean, unmodified identity path from the loss to every block, so gradients stay better behaved and warmup becomes less critical (Xiong et al., 2020). The price is that the stream's magnitude grows with depth (each block adds to it), so late-layer branches matter less, a known weakness of pre-norm for very deep models. DeepNorm (Wang et al., 2022) keeps post-norm but scales the skip path by a constant α > 1 and initialises the branch weights with a matching factor β < 1, both chosen from theory so the update size per layer is bounded; it allowed training transformers 1,000 layers deep. All of these are the same idea: keep the accumulated gain across depth near 1 by controlling the ratio between the identity path and the branches.

Adam changes which symptom hurts

With plain SGD, a parameter's step is proportional to its gradient, so a layer whose gradients are 10⁴ times smaller than another's moves 10⁴ times more slowly at the same learning rate — vanishing gradients translate directly into non-learning. Adam (dl5) divides each parameter's gradient by the running root-mean-square of its recent gradients, so the step is about η regardless of the gradient's absolute size, as long as the gradient stays well above the stabiliser ε (10⁻⁸ by default). Consequently, a well-scaled but low-magnitude gradient — early layers of a deep network — still produces normal-sized updates. Two caveats keep this from being a cure. If the forward signal has vanished, the early layers see almost no information from the input, and the normalised gradient is mostly noise. And ε is a floor: gradients around 10⁻²⁰, as in the sigmoid row of the lab, are ignored in either optimiser. This is also why adaptive optimisers made bad initialisations and un-normalised networks survivable in practice — and why the underlying causes still deserve fixing.

Loss spikes in large-model training

At LLM scale, the failure is usually not a permanent explosion but recurring spikes. PaLM's authors report that their largest model spiked about 20 times "despite the fact that gradient clipping was enabled", at irregular intervals, sometimes late in training, and never in the smaller models. They did not find a principled cure; the mitigation was to restart from a checkpoint about 100 steps before the spike and skip roughly 200–500 batches, after which the loss did not spike again at that point. Their ablation is the interesting part: training on the same batches from a different earlier checkpoint did not spike, so it was not "bad data" alone but the combination of specific batches and a particular parameter state. Wortsman et al. (2023) reproduced two well-known sources of instability at small scale: growth of attention logits (the query–key dot products become large so softmax saturates and its gradient vanishes or spikes) and divergence of the output logits from the log-probabilities. They showed that both appear at high learning rates and are cured by the same stabilisers used at scale: QK-layernorm (normalise queries and keys before the dot product) and an auxiliary z-loss on the softmax normaliser (PaLM used 10⁻⁴·log²Z). Other levers: a lower peak learning rate or longer warmup, a lower Adam β₂ (0.95 rather than 0.999 makes the second-moment estimate react faster after a distribution shift), and a bigger ε to avoid dividing by near-zero in rarely updated parameters.

Adaptive gradient clipping and scale invariance

Global-norm clipping uses one absolute threshold for the whole model, which is awkward if layers differ in scale or if the batch size changes. Adaptive gradient clipping (Brock et al., NFNets) clips a unit's gradient when the ratio of its gradient norm to its weight norm exceeds a threshold, so the allowed step is proportional to the weights being changed — the same idea as the update-to-weight ratio. It made possible training large-batch networks without batch normalisation. Relatedly, a layer followed by a normaliser is scale-invariant: multiplying its weights by c does not change the output, so the gradient scales as 1/c and the effective learning rate of a layer depends on its weight norm; weight decay and growing weight norms therefore interact with the gradient scale in ways that show up as slowly drifting gradient norms.

Precision limits

Vanishing has a numerical twin: a gradient smaller than the smallest representable number is exactly zero. In float16 the smallest normal number is about 6×10⁻⁵ (subnormals reach 6×10⁻⁸), so small gradients underflow even in networks that are fine in float32; loss scaling multiplies the loss so gradients sit in the representable range. bfloat16 has float32's exponent range and normally needs none (gpu4). Explosion has an overflow twin: float16 tops out at 65,504, so a gradient that is merely large in float32 becomes inf in float16. The mixed-precision scaler treats non-finite gradients as a signal to skip the step and reduce the scale, which is why a few skipped steps at the start of an fp16 run are normal and a continuing stream of them is not.
prod:
The public case: ResNet and the degradation problem

In 2015 Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren and Jian Sun at Microsoft Research wanted to know whether deeper image classifiers were simply better if they could be trained, and found they could not, quite. "Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition" (arXiv:1512.03385) opens with the observation that as networks get deeper, accuracy saturates and then degrades, and that "such degradation is not caused by overfitting": the deeper plain network has higher training error. Their fix was to let each block learn a residual on top of an identity shortcut. The numbers (all from the paper): on ImageNet, an 18-layer plain network had 27.94% top-1 validation error and a 34-layer plain network 28.54% — worse. The same two architectures with shortcuts (ResNet-18 and ResNet-34) reached 27.88% and 25.03%, and the deeper one now won. Going deeper still with bottleneck blocks, a single 152-layer ResNet reached 4.49% top-5 validation error, and an ensemble of residual nets achieved 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet test set, winning the ILSVRC 2015 classification task. The 152-layer network is 8× deeper than VGG-19 but has lower complexity: 11.3 billion FLOPs versus 19.6 billion.

On CIFAR-10 (small 32×32 images) they trained 20-, 32-, 44- and 56-layer plain networks and residual ones: the plain networks got worse with depth, the residual ones better. A 110-layer ResNet with 1.7 million parameters reached 6.43% test error (best of five runs; mean 6.61%), and a 1,202-layer network with 19.4 million parameters trained "with no optimization difficulty" to a training error below 0.1% but a test error of 7.93%, worse than the 110-layer model, which the authors attribute to overfitting: even that record-setting depth was not free. One footnote is a nice illustration of this lesson: the 110-layer network needed a warm-up phase at learning rate 0.01, because an initial 0.1 was "slightly too large to start converging".

The section most relevant to this topic is what they say about vanishing gradients: they note that vanishing/exploding gradients had been "largely addressed by normalized initialization and intermediate normalization layers", tested the plain nets with batch normalisation, verified healthy forward and backward norms, and concluded the optimisation difficulty is "unlikely to be caused by vanishing gradients". For an interview, this is the key nuance: residual connections made very deep networks trainable, the mechanism is a better-conditioned optimisation problem with a clean gain-1 path, and the paper itself does not claim it is about vanishing gradients in the narrow sense.

Loss spikes in production LLM runs

PaLM's account (Chowdhery et al., 2022, section 5.1) is the best-documented public example of gradient instability at scale: about 20 spikes in the largest model despite global-norm clipping at 1.0 and a z-loss, handled by rewinding roughly 100 steps and skipping 200–500 batches. The operational lessons: keep checkpoints frequent enough to rewind (the cost of a rewind is the time since the last checkpoint plus the data skipped); log the batch identifiers seen at each step so a spike can be replayed; and automate the skip-and-restart procedure since large runs run for weeks and spikes at 3 a.m. should not need a human.

What to monitor and how

At minimum, log every step: the training loss, the pre-clip global gradient norm, the fraction of steps where clipping engaged, the learning rate, and (for fp16) the loss-scale value and the count of skipped steps. Every few hundred steps, log per-layer gradient norms, per-layer weight norms and the update-to-weight ratio lr × ‖grad‖ / ‖weight‖, typically about 10⁻³ in a healthy run: a layer at 10⁻⁶ is barely learning; one at 10⁻¹ is unstable. Plot them as a heat map (layer on one axis, step on the other) to see drift and spikes at a glance. A gradient-norm spike that precedes a loss spike by a few steps is the classic signature and can trigger an automatic alert or a batch skip.

def layer_stats(model):
    for name, p in model.named_parameters():
        if p.grad is not None:
            ratio = (p.grad.norm() * lr) / (p.norm() + 1e-12)
            yield name, p.grad.norm().item(), ratio.item()

Failure modes in practice

NaN from one bad batch. A single example with an extreme value, an empty target sequence (division by zero in a mean) or a corrupted image can produce a non-finite gradient. Use clip_grad_norm_(..., error_if_nonfinite=True) or check torch.isfinite(gnorm) and skip the optimiser step when it fails; a run that silently applies a NaN update is unrecoverable, while a skipped step costs nothing. Log the batch identifiers of skipped steps.

Clipping that hides a problem. If the pre-clip norm is above the threshold on most steps, clipping has become part of the optimiser, effectively rescaling the learning rate: the true diagnosis is that the threshold is too low or the model is unstable. Track the clipped fraction and treat a sustained value above a few percent as a warning.

Warm restarts that forget optimiser state. Resuming from a checkpoint without Adam's moments makes the first steps huge (the second-moment estimate is empty), which looks exactly like a gradient explosion at the resume step. Restore optimiser state and the step counter (dl1, dl5).

Depth added without re-tuning. Adding layers to a working residual model changes the accumulated branch variance; the learning rate that worked at 12 layers may spike at 48. Scale branch initialisation with depth (the 1/√N rule) and re-run a short learning-rate sweep rather than assuming transfer.
myths: Vanishing gradients are only a problem for sigmoid and tanh; ReLU solved them.

ReLU removes the activation-slope factor on active paths, but the gradient is still a product of weight matrices. In the lab, a 30-layer ReLU network with the wrong weight scale lost a factor of about 4,000 (variance-halving init) or gained a factor of about 100,000 (too-large init) between the top and the bottom layer. Depth makes any per-layer factor other than 1 exponential, whatever the activation.
Exploding gradients happen when the weights are large, so bigger weights always mean bigger gradients.

In a saturating network the opposite can happen. With tanh, large weights push units into the flat regions where the slope is nearly zero, so the gradient vanishes: in a 10-layer scalar chain with weight 2.5 the end-to-end gradient was 7×10⁻¹¹, smaller than with weight 0.5 (9×10⁻⁴). Explosion needs both large weight gain and units staying in their sensitive region, which is typical of ReLU and recurrent networks.
Gradient clipping fixes vanishing gradients too.

Clipping only scales a gradient down when its norm exceeds a threshold, so it cannot lift a tiny gradient. It is a guard against rare huge gradients (bad batches, loss spikes), and large-model runs use it routinely, but the cures for vanishing are initialisation, normalisation, residual connections and gating.
Residual connections make gradient problems disappear entirely.

They guarantee a path with gain 1, but stacking many residual blocks adds their contributions, so the signal and gradient can grow with depth. In the lab, a 30-layer residual ReLU network initialised like the plain one had a 7.7-million-fold larger gradient at the first layer than at the last; scaling each branch's weights by 1/√depth brought it back to about 17. Real transformers use exactly that kind of residual scaling.
The ResNet paper showed that residual connections cure vanishing gradients.

The paper argues something more careful: its plain 34-layer networks used batch normalisation, and the authors verified that forward signals and backward gradients had healthy norms, yet the deeper plain network still had higher training error than the 18-layer one. They called this the degradation problem, an optimisation difficulty that vanishing gradients do not explain, and showed that residual learning fixed it.
Adam makes vanishing gradients irrelevant because it rescales each parameter's step.

It helps with one symptom: because Adam divides by the running root-mean-square gradient, a layer with gradients 10,000× smaller still takes normal-sized steps (as long as they stay well above Adam's ε ≈ 10⁻⁸). But if the forward signal has vanished, the layers see almost no information, and the gradient's direction becomes noise. Adam is a bandage on the symptom, not a substitute for a well-scaled architecture.
lab:
Goal: measure vanishing and exploding gradients directly. The script builds a plain 30-layer, width-100 network with hand-written forward and backward passes (the same rules as dl1), records how large the gradient is when it reaches each layer, and compares initialisations, activations and residual connections; it then demonstrates global-norm clipping. NumPy only, Python 3.12, runs in a few seconds.

import numpy as np

DEPTH, WIDTH, BATCH = 30, 100, 64
ACT = {
    "sigmoid": (lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)), lambda z, a: a * (1 - a)),
    "tanh":    (np.tanh,                        lambda z, a: 1 - a ** 2),
    "relu":    (lambda z: np.maximum(z, 0),     lambda z, a: (z > 0).astype(float)),
}

def run(act, std, residual=False, seed=0):
    """Forward + backward through DEPTH layers.
    Returns (backward signal size at each layer, weight-gradient norm of each layer), input side first."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    f, df = ACT[act]
    Ws = [r.normal(0, std, (WIDTH, WIDTH)) for _ in range(DEPTH)]
    h, cache = r.normal(size=(BATCH, WIDTH)), []
    for W in Ws:                                     # forward: keep inputs, pre-activations, outputs
        z = h @ W; a = f(z)
        cache.append((h, z, a))
        h = h + a if residual else a
    d = np.ones_like(h) / h.size                     # dL/dh at the top (loss = mean of the output)
    sig, wg = [], []
    for W, (hin, z, a) in zip(reversed(Ws), reversed(cache)):
        dz = d * df(z, a)
        wg.append(np.linalg.norm(hin.T @ dz))        # weight gradient: (layer input)ᵀ · dz
        d = dz @ W.T + (d if residual else 0)        # gradient handed to the layer below (+ skip path)
        sig.append(np.linalg.norm(d))
    return sig[::-1], wg[::-1]

print("depth 30, width 100.  'signal' = size of the gradient reaching a layer's input, relative to the top layer")
print(f"{'setup':34} {'signal @L1':>11} {'signal @L15':>12} {'weight-grad @L1':>16}")
setups = [("sigmoid, N(0, 0.1)", "sigmoid", 0.1, False),
          ("tanh, std 0.05 (too small)", "tanh", 0.05, False),
          ("tanh, Xavier 1/sqrt(n)", "tanh", 1 / np.sqrt(WIDTH), False),
          ("tanh, std 0.25 (too big)", "tanh", 0.25, False),
          ("relu, 1/sqrt(n) (too small)", "relu", 1 / np.sqrt(WIDTH), False),
          ("relu, He sqrt(2/n)", "relu", np.sqrt(2 / WIDTH), False),
          ("relu, 2/sqrt(n) (too big)", "relu", 2 / np.sqrt(WIDTH), False),
          ("relu, He + residual (unscaled)", "relu", np.sqrt(2 / WIDTH), True),
          ("relu, He/sqrt(L) + residual", "relu", np.sqrt(2 / WIDTH / DEPTH), True)]
for label, act, std, res in setups:
    sig, wg = run(act, std, res)
    top = sig[-1]
    print(f"{label:34} {sig[0]/top:11.1e} {sig[14]/top:12.1e} {wg[0]:16.1e}")

# ---- gradient clipping by global norm: direction is kept, length is capped
def clip(grads, max_norm=1.0):
    total = np.sqrt(sum((g ** 2).sum() for g in grads))
    return [g * min(1.0, max_norm / (total + 1e-6)) for g in grads], total
g = [np.array([3.0, 4.0]), np.array([12.0])]            # global norm = sqrt(9 + 16 + 144) = 13
clipped, total = clip(g)
print("\nglobal norm before clipping:", round(float(total), 2),
      " after:", round(float(np.sqrt(sum((c ** 2).sum() for c in clipped))), 3))
print("clipped grads:", [c.round(3).tolist() for c in clipped])

What to look for.

  1. The table's "signal @L1" column is the size of the gradient reaching layer 1 relative to the top layer. Sigmoid with a modest init loses about 19 orders of magnitude; tanh with σ = 0.05 loses 9 (0.5³⁰ ≈ 9×10⁻¹⁰, exactly the per-layer gain of 0.5 the theory predicts); tanh with Xavier σ = 1/√n stays near 0.1; a too-large tanh init grows by about a thousand.
  2. ReLU rows. He initialisation (σ = √(2/n)) keeps the ratio within a factor of a few of 1; the "Xavier-like" 1/√n loses a factor of about 4,000 and 2/√n gains about 100,000. The difference between the last two is a factor of two in the standard deviation of the weights.
  3. Weight-gradient column. For the too-small tanh network the first layer's weight gradient is about 10⁻¹⁰ in absolute terms: it is the product of a tiny backward signal and a tiny layer input (activations shrink too, going up), which is also why comparing weight-gradient norms across layers can look deceptively flat.
  4. Residual rows. Adding skip connections without scaling the branches does not help: the gradient at layer 1 is 8 million times that at layer 30. Scaling the branch weights by 1/√L (30) brings it back to about 17. Try replacing 1/√L with 1/L and watch what happens to the ratio.
  5. The clipping demo prints a global norm of 13.0 before clipping and 1.0 after, with gradients (3, 4, 12) → (0.231, 0.308, 0.923) — direction preserved, as in the lesson.

Try next. Sweep the width (50, 100, 400) at a fixed σ: the critical σ scales like 1/√n, so what is stable at one width explodes at another. Add batch normalisation to each layer's output and see how much less the ratio depends on σ.
recap: The gradient reaching layer 1 is a product of one Jacobian factor per layer above it; if the typical factor (gain) is below 1 it shrinks exponentially with depth, above 1 it grows exponentially, and only a gain very close to 1 survives: 0.8⁴⁹ ≈ 2×10⁻⁵ while 1.2⁴⁹ ≈ 7,600.

For a random layer with weights of variance σ² and width n, the gain on a vector is about σ√n, so the critical initialisation is σ² = 1/n for linear or tanh-like layers (Xavier uses 2/(n_in + n_out)) and 2/n for ReLU, which zeroes half its inputs (He).

The same product structure governs forward activations and backward gradients, so a good initialisation keeps both roughly constant across layers; the wrong scale makes both shrink or both grow together.

Sigmoid and tanh add a slope below 1 at every layer and saturate; ReLU removes the slope factor, but weights still matter, so activation choice, initialisation and normalisation have to be chosen together.

Residual connections make each block compute x + f(x), so the layer's Jacobian is I + J_f and the gradient always has an identity path back; most of the gradient in a 110-layer ResNet travels through paths only 10–34 layers deep.

Residual sums still accumulate, so transformers scale the initialisation of residual output projections (about 1/√(number of residual layers)) or normalise before each block to keep the stream's size in check.
Gated recurrent units (LSTM, GRU) give the recurrent state an additive, gated path across time steps, the temporal counterpart of a residual connection.

Gradient clipping by global norm rescales the whole gradient when its norm exceeds a threshold (typically 1.0) while preserving its direction; it stops explosions and loss spikes but does nothing for vanishing gradients.
Diagnose by logging per-layer gradient norms and the update-to-weight ratio: a steep decline toward the input means vanishing, a steep rise or spiking global norm means exploding.

drill:
Work it out

A 50-layer network where every layer's Jacobian has typical gain s. Compute the gradient scale reaching layer 1 for s = 0.8 and s = 1.2, then say what a residual connection changes.

Answer

The gradient at layer 1 passes through 49 Jacobians, so it is scaled by s⁴⁹.

s = 0.8: 0.8⁴⁹ ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Layer 1 receives a gradient about 55,000 times smaller than layer 50, so with a shared learning rate it effectively never trains.

s = 1.2: 1.2⁴⁹ ≈ 7.6 × 10³. The gradient is thousands of times larger at layer 1; with a learning rate that suits the last layers, the first ones take enormous steps, and in float16 (maximum 65,504) intermediate values can overflow to infinity within a few steps.

The survivable band is narrow: a 20% deviation from 1.0 in either direction is fatal at 50 layers, because depth turns a small multiplicative bias into an exponential one.

What residuals change: with x + f(x), each layer's Jacobian becomes I + J_f. The identity term guarantees a path on which the product stays at 1 no matter how small J_f is, so gradients can flow straight to the input. If the branches are small (say J_f has norm 0.01) the total gain over 50 blocks is about 1.01⁵⁰ ≈ 1.6: harmless. The caution: if the branches are not small, their contributions add up and can explode (1.2⁴⁹ again), which is why residual branches are initialised small or zero and why pre-norm and depth-dependent scaling exist.

Clipping does not help here. It caps explosion; it cannot lift a vanished gradient. A different problem needs a different fix.

Diagnose it

You log the global gradient norm every step for a 24-layer transformer. It sits around 0.4, then over 30 steps climbs to 3 with the loss still falling, and at step 8,200 the norm jumps to 60 and the loss to 12 before slowly recovering. Your clip threshold is 1.0. What is likely happening, and what do you do?

Answer

Reading the log. The slow climb from 0.4 to 3 suggests a growing instability (growing weights or attention logits) rather than a one-off. The jump to 60 is a spike: at that step every gradient was scaled by 1/60, so the update was safely small in size but was still in the direction of one enormous gradient, which is why the loss went to 12. Clipping bounded the step's length; it did not remove the cause, and once the norm exceeded 1.0 for many steps the clipped fraction had already been high (the whole "0.4 to 3" period), meaning the optimiser was being throttled.

What to do, in order: (1) find the batch at step 8,200 — replay it from a checkpoint before the spike; if it spikes only from that parameter state, it is the combination effect seen in PaLM. (2) Check the trend in per-layer norms and attention-logit magnitudes to see which layer grows. (3) Apply the stabilisers: QK-normalisation, a z-loss on the output logits, a lower peak learning rate or longer warmup, a slightly lower Adam β₂, bf16 if the run is fp16. (4) Operationally: rewind to a checkpoint before the climb began and skip the offending batches, as PaLM did. (5) Re-tune the clip threshold using the healthy 0.4 as the typical scale, e.g. 1.0 is fine but 0.5 would have engaged earlier during the climb.

The habit to state in an interview: alert on the pre-clip gradient norm's trend, not only on the loss.
qa: E
What are vanishing and exploding gradients, in plain words?

Backprop multiplies one factor per layer as the gradient travels from the loss back to the early layers. If those factors are typically below 1, the product shrinks exponentially and the early layers receive almost no learning signal; if they are above 1, it grows exponentially and updates blow up to NaN. Thirty factors of 0.5 give about 10⁻⁹; thirty factors of 1.5 give about 190,000.
E
How can you tell from a training run that gradients are vanishing or exploding?

Log the gradient norm per layer and the global gradient norm. Vanishing shows as norms falling by orders of magnitude toward the input layers, early-layer weights that barely change, and a loss that stalls. Exploding shows as a spiking or rapidly growing global norm, a loss that jumps or turns NaN, and weights growing large. The update-to-weight ratio (about 10⁻³ per step is healthy) is a good complement.
E
Does gradient clipping fix vanishing gradients?

No. Clipping only caps large gradients, so it addresses explosion. Vanishing needs a change to the architecture or initialisation: residual connections, normalisation, a variance-preserving initialisation, or gating. Clipping is still standard insurance in large training runs against a single bad batch.
M
Why does He initialisation use a factor of two compared with Xavier?

For a layer with n inputs and weight variance σ², the pre-activation variance is about n·σ²·E[x²]; keeping it constant needs σ² = 1/n. ReLU sets the negative half of its inputs to zero, so the second moment of its output is half that of its input, and doubling the weight variance to 2/n compensates. Xavier's 2/(fan_in + fan_out) assumes an activation that is roughly linear near zero, such as tanh, and undershoots for ReLU: in a 30-layer test a 1/n init lost a factor of about 4,000 in gradient between top and bottom while 2/n kept it near 6.
M
Why do residual connections help train very deep networks?

A residual block computes x + f(x), so its Jacobian is I + J_f. The identity term means the gradient always has a path with gain 1 back to earlier layers, whatever the block's own gradient does, instead of only a product of many possibly small factors. Veit et al. showed a residual network behaves like an ensemble of paths of different lengths, and in a 110-layer ResNet most of the gradient flows through paths only 10–34 layers deep. Residual nets also let a block start close to the identity, which is an easier place to begin optimising.

Follow-up: Do they solve every gradient problem? — No; branch outputs add up with depth, so the residual stream can grow, and models scale the branch initialisation (about 1/√N) or normalise before the branch to control it.
M
What is the difference between clipping by value and clipping by global norm, and which do you use?

Clipping by value caps each gradient component separately, which changes the gradient's direction. Clipping by global norm computes the norm of all gradients together and, if it exceeds a threshold, multiplies every gradient by threshold/norm; the direction is preserved and only the length is capped. For example a gradient of (3, 4, 12) has norm 13 and with a threshold of 1 becomes (0.23, 0.31, 0.92). LLM recipes use global-norm clipping at 1.0 (LLaMA, PaLM).

Follow-up: How do you choose the threshold? — Log the pre-clip norm for a stable run; set the threshold near the typical value or a bit above so clipping fires only on spikes, and track the fraction of steps clipped.
M
Why can large weights cause vanishing rather than exploding gradients in a tanh network?

Large weights push pre-activations far from zero, into the flat regions of tanh where the slope is close to 0, so each layer multiplies the gradient by a tiny slope. The weight gain is large but the slope gain is far below 1, and the product vanishes. In a 10-layer scalar tanh chain a weight of 2.5 gave an end-to-end gradient of 7×10⁻¹¹ versus 9×10⁻⁴ for a weight of 0.5. Explosion in such networks needs units to stay in the sensitive region, which is why it is more typical of ReLU and recurrent networks.
M
How do LSTMs address vanishing gradients in a way plain RNNs do not?

A plain RNN multiplies by the same recurrent matrix (and an activation slope) at every time step, so the gradient over T steps scales like the matrix's spectral radius to the power T. The LSTM's cell state is updated additively, c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t−1} + i_t ⊙ g_t, so with the forget gate near 1 the gradient flows back through an approximately identity path. It is the recurrent ancestor of the residual connection: same idea, an additive path with gain about 1.
Follow-up: Do LSTMs also explode? — Yes, they can, which is why gradient clipping is standard in recurrent training (Pascanu et al.).
H
Your 40-layer plain ReLU network has loss stuck at its initial value. How do you diagnose and fix it?

First overfit a single batch to rule out bugs. Then measure the per-layer gradient and activation norms at initialisation: if both shrink toward the input, the init is too small or a saturating activation is used; if the gradient falls but activations are healthy, suspect dead ReLUs or a detached branch. Fix in order of preference: switch to He initialisation for ReLU, add normalisation (batch, layer, RMS), add residual connections, lower the depth or learning rate, and use warmup. Then re-check the norms are roughly flat across layers.

Follow-up: What if the loss is fine but early layers learn slowly? — Check the update-to-weight ratio per layer; with Adam the per-parameter normalisation may already compensate, and layer-wise learning rates or better scaling can help.
H
The ResNet paper reports that a 56-layer plain network had higher training error than a 20-layer one. Is that vanishing gradients?

Not according to the authors. Their plain networks used batch normalisation, and they verified that forward signals had non-zero variance and backward gradients had healthy norms, so neither signal vanished; they also found the 34-layer plain network could still reach competitive accuracy. They named it the degradation problem: an optimisation difficulty in which a deeper network, which could in principle copy the shallower one and add identity layers, is harder to optimise than the shallow one. Residual learning lets extra layers default to the identity, and the training error then falls with depth (plain-34 28.54% versus ResNet-34 25.03% top-1 on ImageNet validation).
H
How do modern LLM recipes control gradient explosion and loss spikes?

Layered defences: pre-normalisation (RMSNorm before each sub-layer) keeps the residual path clean; small residual-branch initialisation (scaled by about 1/√number of layers, as in GPT-2); learning-rate warmup; AdamW with β₂ around 0.95–0.999 and global-norm clipping at 1.0; an auxiliary z-loss to keep output logits bounded (PaLM used 10⁻⁴·log²Z); QK-normalisation and logit soft-capping in some models to stop attention logits growing; and bfloat16 to avoid overflow. Even so, PaLM's largest run had about 20 loss spikes despite clipping, handled by restarting from a checkpoint roughly 100 steps earlier and skipping 200–500 batches.

Follow-up: Were the spikes caused by bad data? — The PaLM authors do not think so: the same batches did not spike when trained from a different earlier checkpoint, so it is the combination of particular batches and a particular parameter state.
H
Explain dynamical isometry and why orthogonal initialisation is used for very deep networks.

Training is well conditioned when the singular values of the input–output Jacobian are all near 1, so gradients neither shrink nor grow along any direction: dynamical isometry. A Gaussian random matrix has singular values spread over a range, so a product of many of them spreads out exponentially even if the average gain is 1. An orthogonal matrix has all singular values exactly 1, so a stack of them preserves lengths exactly; combined with a suitable activation and scaling, Xiao et al. trained vanilla CNNs 10,000 layers deep without residual connections or normalisation. In practice residual connections and normalisation are far easier, so orthogonal init matters mainly for recurrent weights and theory.

sum: How BatchNorm, LayerNorm and RMSNorm standardise activations over different axes, worked on a 2×3 tensor with real numbers, why CNNs use the batch axis and transformers do not, the train/eval trap, pre-norm vs post-norm, and where each shows up in modern LLMs.
prereq: dl3
Gradients scale with the product of per-layer gains, so a layer's output scale matters; normalisation keeps that scale near 1 at every layer regardless of the weights below.
ml4
Standardising input features (zero mean, unit variance) fixes ill-conditioned loss surfaces and lets gradient descent use a larger learning rate.
dl2
ReLU and other activations are sensitive to the scale of their input: saturating ones vanish at large scale and ReLU networks need a matching initial variance.
why:
In 2014 Google's best image classifier, Inception, took about 31 million training steps to reach 72.2% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet. Its authors could not simply turn up the learning rate to speed things up: a five-fold increase made the model's parameters "reach machine infinity" — training exploded. They could not use sigmoid activations either; the network never got better than one-in-a-thousand chance accuracy. Everything about that network was delicate: the initial weights, the learning rate, the choice of activation. Then Sergey Ioffe and Christian Szegedy added one small operation between layers, and the same network matched its old accuracy in 2.1 million steps with a five-times-higher learning rate — fourteen times fewer steps — and even trained with sigmoids.

The operation is normalisation: after a layer computes its outputs, subtract their mean and divide by their standard deviation, so the next layer always receives numbers on a standard scale, then let the network learn its preferred scale and shift. It sounds too simple to matter. But recall dl3: the gradient reaching the early layers is a product of one factor per layer, and each factor depends on the scale of that layer's weights and activations. A normalisation layer resets the scale at every depth, so the product cannot drift away from 1 however the weights below it change. That single change removed much of the fragility of deep networks, and it is now in almost every architecture you will meet.

The subtlety — and the reason this is a favourite interview topic — is that there are several versions and they are not interchangeable. BatchNorm, the original, normalises across the examples in a batch; it works wonderfully for image networks but has a training mode and an evaluation mode, fails with tiny batches, and is awkward with variable-length text. Transformers use LayerNorm or, in modern large language models, RMSNorm, which normalise across the features of each example on its own. And where you put the normalisation inside a transformer block (before or after the sub-layer) decides whether a deep model trains stably. Getting these details right is what separates "I've heard of BatchNorm" from being able to debug a model that behaves differently in evaluation than in training.

This lesson builds all of it from the ground up. We start from why standardising inputs helped in the first place (ml4) and extend it to hidden layers, then work every variant by hand on a 2×3 tensor with real numbers so the axis difference is unmistakable. We cover BatchNorm's running statistics and the train/eval trap, derive the gradient of a normalisation layer and what it implies, discuss why normalisation helps (with an honest account of the debate), compare LayerNorm and RMSNorm, examine GroupNorm and the small-batch failure, and place the norm inside a transformer block. The public case is the original BatchNorm paper, whose numbers we check against the source, and the lab shows a 30-layer network becoming insensitive to its initialisation.
primer:
Grading on a curve — two ways

Imagine a school where 200 students each take the same exam of 10 questions, and you want to put everyone's scores on a common scale. There are two natural ways to "grade on a curve". You can standardise each question across all the students: for question 3, compute the average score and the spread over the 200 students, and convert every student's score on that question to "how many spreads above or below the average". Or you can standardise each student across all their questions: for student 17, compute the average and spread over their 10 answers and convert each to a standardised score.

These two are BatchNorm and LayerNorm. Picture a table of activations in which each row is one example in the batch (a student) and each column is one feature (a question). BatchNorm computes a mean and variance down each column, pooling over the batch. LayerNorm computes them along each row, pooling over the features of a single example. RMSNorm is LayerNorm that skips the subtraction of the mean and only divides by a measure of size. The analogy holds well; where it needs care is that in a real network the "questions" are learned features whose meaning changes as training proceeds, which is why the layer keeps adapting.

The recipe

Every variant applies the same two steps to the numbers in one pooled set:

normalised = (x − mean) / √(variance + ε)        step 1: standardise (ε ≈ 1e-5 avoids dividing by zero)
output     = γ × normalised + β                   step 2: learned scale γ and shift β, one pair per feature

Step 2 matters. If the layer only standardised, every layer's output would be forced to mean 0 and variance 1, which would restrict what the next layer sees. γ (gain) and β (bias) are learned like any weights, so the network can restore any scale and offset it prefers — including exactly undoing the standardisation. What normalisation adds is that the output scale is now controlled by two dedicated numbers instead of by every weight in every layer below.

A first worked example

One example's features are (2, 4, 6). LayerNorm: mean = 4; the squared deviations are 4, 0, 4, so variance = 8/3 ≈ 2.67 and standard deviation ≈ 1.63; the normalised values are (2−4)/1.63, 0, (6−4)/1.63 = (−1.22, 0, 1.22). RMSNorm skips the mean: the root-mean-square is √((4 + 16 + 36)/3) = √18.67 ≈ 4.32, giving (2, 4, 6)/4.32 = (0.46, 0.93, 1.39). Same idea, slightly different result: LayerNorm centres the numbers on zero, RMSNorm only rescales them.

Which to use, briefly

Convolutional networks for images: BatchNorm (or GroupNorm when batches are small). Transformers and recurrent networks: LayerNorm or RMSNorm, because they do not depend on other examples in the batch. Modern LLMs: RMSNorm, applied before each sub-layer. The rest of the lesson explains why, and the traps that come with each.
body:
1. Why normalise at all

Recall from ml4 that gradient descent on a loss whose features have wildly different scales converges slowly: the loss surface is a long narrow valley, the stable learning rate is set by the steep direction, and progress along the shallow one crawls. Centring and scaling the input features fixes this, which is why we standardise data before training. Inside a deep network the same problem reappears at every layer: the input to layer 7 is the output of layer 6, and its scale and offset depend on layer 6's weights, which keep changing. If layer 6's outputs drift to values around 100 (or 0.001), layer 7 sees a differently scaled problem, a saturating activation may be pushed into its flat region, and ReLU units may all switch off. Initialisation (dl3) sets the scales right at step 0 but cannot keep them right afterwards. Normalisation is the mechanism that maintains the scale throughout training: standardise each layer's inputs inside the network, on every forward pass.

2. BatchNorm, step by step

Take a mini-batch of m examples and one feature (one column of the table). BatchNorm (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015) computes, for that feature:

  1. the batch mean μ = (1/m) Σ xᵢ;
  2. the batch variance σ² = (1/m) Σ (xᵢ − μ)²;
  3. the normalised values x̂ᵢ = (xᵢ − μ)/√(σ² + ε);
  4. the output yᵢ = γ x̂ᵢ + β, where γ and β are learned parameters for this feature.

In a convolutional layer the "feature" is a channel, and the statistics pool over the batch and all spatial positions (m × H × W values per channel), with one γ and β per channel. Worked on a single column: the four values (2, 4, 6, 8) have mean 5 and variance ((−3)² + (−1)² + 1² + 3²)/4 = 5, so σ = 2.236 and the normalised values are (−1.342, −0.447, 0.447, 1.342): mean 0, variance 1. With γ = 1 and β = 0 that is the output; with γ = 2 and β = 1 it would be (−1.68, 0.11, 1.89, 3.68).

The full 2×3 example. Now the smallest table that shows both axes: two examples, three features, X = [[2, 4, 6], [0, 3, 9]].

row 1row 2how it is computed
BatchNorm (per column)(1, 1, −1)(−1, −1, 1)column means (1, 3.5, 7.5), column variances (1, 0.25, 2.25)
LayerNorm (per row)(−1.225, 0, 1.225)(−1.069, −0.267, 1.336)row means (4, 4), row variances (2.67, 14)
RMSNorm (per row)(0.463, 0.926, 1.389)(0, 0.548, 1.643)row RMS (4.32, 5.48)

Look at what each does. LayerNorm's output for row 1 depends only on row 1: change the other example and nothing happens. BatchNorm's output for row 1 is (1, 1, −1) only because row 2 exists, and with a batch of just two examples every output is exactly ±1 — the layer can say only "larger or smaller than my batch-mate" for each feature, throwing away magnitude. That is an extreme case, but it explains the general behaviour: BatchNorm's output for an example depends on its batch-mates, and the estimate of the statistics gets noisier as the batch shrinks (section 8). RMSNorm preserves the sign pattern of its input (row 2 stays non-negative, since the inputs were), while LayerNorm forces zero mean. The lab prints all three so you can check them.

3. BatchNorm at inference: running statistics and the train/eval trap

At inference you may have one example, or a batch of unrelated requests, and you want each prediction to be deterministic and independent of the others. Batch statistics are then wrong for the job. BatchNorm therefore keeps running averages of the mean and variance during training, updated every step with a momentum of (by default in PyTorch) 0.1: running = 0.9 × running + 0.1 × batch_statistic. Starting from running mean 0 and variance 1, after one batch (2, 4, 6, 8) the running mean is 0.9 × 0 + 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 and the running variance is 0.9 × 1 + 0.1 × 6.67 = 1.57. (PyTorch stores the unbiased variance, dividing by m − 1 = 3, i.e. 6.67, in the running estimate, but uses the biased m-divisor for the normalisation itself.) After enough batches the running estimates converge to the population mean and variance. In evaluation mode the layer uses these stored numbers as constants, so the whole layer becomes a fixed per-channel affine map: y = γ (x − running_mean) / √(running_var + ε) + β.

This design produces a set of classic bugs, each worth being able to explain:

  • Forgetting model.eval() before validation or inference: BatchNorm keeps using (and updating) batch statistics, so predictions depend on batch composition and are noisier; a model that trained well appears to have poor accuracy.
  • Batch size 1 in training mode: the batch mean equals the single value, the variance is 0, so x − μ = 0 and the output is exactly β for every input. All information is destroyed. (In eval mode, batch size 1 is perfectly fine.)
  • Domain shift: running statistics reflect the training data. If serving data looks different (new camera, different resolution), they are wrong; re-estimating them on target data (AdaBN) is a cheap fix.
  • Small-batch fine-tuning: fine-tuning a pretrained model with a batch of 2–4 makes the running statistics drift to noisy estimates within a few dozen steps (0.9ⁿ decays quickly), so evaluation, which uses them, degrades. Standard remedy: freeze BatchNorm (keep it in eval mode) during fine-tuning of detection and segmentation models.
  • Data-parallel training: each GPU sees only its own slice of the batch, so statistics are per-GPU. SyncBatchNorm computes them across all GPUs at the price of an all-reduce per layer (gpu8).

4. What normalisation does to gradients

Since normalisation is inside the network, backprop (dl1) must go through it. Write the layer for one set of activations as x̂ = (x − μ)/σ, y = γ x̂ + β. The gradient with respect to the input, for upstream gradient dy and taking γ = 1 for clarity, is:

dx = (1/σ) · ( dy − mean(dy) − x̂ · mean(dy ⊙ x̂) )

Read it in words. The gradient is divided by σ, so if the input is large the gradient is correspondingly small (that is the automatic scale adjustment: gradients no longer depend on how large the activations below happen to be). And two terms are subtracted: mean(dy) removes the component of the gradient along the constant direction (adding a constant to every input changes nothing, since the mean is subtracted), and x̂ · mean(dy ⊙ x̂) removes the component along x̂ itself (multiplying the input by a constant changes nothing, since the variance is divided out). Worked with LayerNorm on (2, 4, 6): x̂ = (−1.225, 0, 1.225), σ = 1.633. For upstream gradient dy = (1, 0, 0): mean(dy) = 0.333; mean(dy ⊙ x̂) = −1.225/3 = −0.408; then dy − 0.333 − x̂ · (−0.408) = (0.667, −0.333, −0.333) − (0.5, 0, −0.5) = (0.167, −0.333, 0.167), and dividing by σ gives (0.102, −0.204, 0.102). Note that it sums to zero. Now try dy = −x̂ = (1.225, 0, −1.225), a gradient that would just make the input larger along its own direction: the formula returns exactly (0, 0, 0). Scaling the input has no effect on the output, so the gradient correctly has no such component. (The lab verifies both numbers with finite differences.)

This has a very useful consequence for training. A normalised layer is scale-invariant: multiplying the weights of the layer below by any positive constant c does not change the output. Two things follow (deep section): the gradient with respect to those weights scales as 1/c and is orthogonal to the weights, so weights tend to grow during training and the effective learning rate (step size relative to weight size, roughly η/‖w‖²) shrinks automatically. That built-in learning-rate adjustment is one reason normalised networks tolerate large learning rates.

5. Why does it help? An honest account

Ioffe and Szegedy motivated BatchNorm by internal covariate shift: as earlier layers change, the distribution of each layer's inputs changes, so each layer has to keep re-adapting; fixing the mean and variance of each layer's inputs should remove this. This is intuitive and was the accepted story for three years. Santurkar et al. (2018) tested it. They trained networks with BatchNorm and then added random noise (with non-zero mean and non-unit variance, different at every step) after each BatchNorm layer, deliberately introducing severe covariate shift; training was barely worse than plain BatchNorm and far better than no BatchNorm. They concluded that "such distributional stability of layer inputs has little to do with the success of BatchNorm" and measured instead that BatchNorm "makes the optimization landscape significantly smoother": the loss and its gradient change less between nearby points, so gradients are more predictive and larger steps are safe. Three accounts are now usually given together:

  • Smoother loss landscape (Santurkar et al.): the loss is better behaved, allowing higher learning rates and faster convergence.
  • Scale invariance and self-tuning learning rate: weights below a normalised layer can grow without changing the function, and their gradients shrink as they do, so the relative step size adapts on its own.
  • Regularisation from batch noise: each example's normalisation depends on which other examples share its batch, which injects noise similar in spirit to dropout; Ioffe and Szegedy found that BatchNorm sometimes made dropout unnecessary.

The honest interview answer is that the exact mechanism is still debated, that the original internal-covariate-shift explanation has been seriously challenged, and that the empirical benefits (higher learning rates, less sensitivity to initialisation, faster and more stable training) are not in doubt.

6. LayerNorm: the batch-independent version

Ba, Kiros and Hinton (2016) introduced LayerNorm for recurrent networks, where BatchNorm is awkward: statistics would have to be kept per time step, and sequences vary in length. LayerNorm normalises over the features of a single example, so for a transformer token vector x of width d:

μ = (1/d) Σⱼ xⱼ          σ² = (1/d) Σⱼ (xⱼ − μ)²          y = γ ⊙ (x − μ)/√(σ² + ε) + β

with γ and β vectors of length d (2d parameters). In a transformer the activations have shape (batch, tokens, d) and LayerNorm computes one mean and variance for each (batch, token) pair, over the d features. Nothing is shared between tokens or examples. That gives it all the properties transformers need:

BatchNormLayerNorm / RMSNorm
Statistics pooled overthe batch (and space) for each channelthe features of each example (and token)
Depends on other examplesyesno
Train vs eval behaviourdifferent (batch vs running stats)identical
Small batch or batch of 1degrades; batch 1 in train mode outputs βunaffected
Variable-length / padded sequencespadding contaminates statisticsper token; padding irrelevant
Cost at inferencecan be folded into the previous linear layerreal work per token (a reduction and a division)
Typical homeCNNstransformers, RNNs

Geometrically, LayerNorm does two projections: it subtracts the mean (projecting the vector onto the hyperplane of zero-sum vectors), then divides by the length (projecting onto a sphere of radius √d), then applies γ and β. Every token vector entering the next layer therefore has the same norm (before γ), which is why attention and feed-forward layers downstream see a stable scale.

7. RMSNorm: drop the mean

Zhang and Sennrich (2019) hypothesised that of LayerNorm's two invariances, re-centring (shift invariance) and re-scaling (scale invariance), only the second matters. RMSNorm removes re-centring:

rms = √( (1/d) Σⱼ xⱼ² + ε )          y = γ ⊙ x / rms          (no mean subtraction, no bias β)

One reduction (a sum of squares) instead of two, no subtraction, and half the parameters (d instead of 2d). Their reported result: comparable quality to LayerNorm with 7–64% less running time depending on the model. On our example, row 1 becomes (0.463, 0.926, 1.389) instead of LayerNorm's (−1.225, 0, 1.225): the direction of the vector is preserved and only its length is set. RMSNorm is the norm in LLaMA (which also uses it in pre-norm position), Gemma and OLMo 2, usually computed in float32 even when the model runs in bfloat16 because the sum of squares of many values loses precision otherwise. In FLOPs the saving is negligible next to the matmuls (LLaMA-7B has only 65 RMSNorm weight vectors — 2 per layer for 32 layers plus one final — about 266,000 parameters in total, 0.004% of the model), but norm layers are memory-bandwidth-bound and run at every layer for every token, so removing a pass over the data and fusing what remains into one kernel is a measurable speed-up (gpu6).

8. GroupNorm and the small-batch failure

BatchNorm's Achilles heel is small batches. Object detection and segmentation models process high-resolution images and often fit only 1–2 images per GPU. With so few samples the batch mean and variance are noisy estimates, and the noise hurts. Wu and He (2018) measured it on ResNet-50 for ImageNet classification: BatchNorm's validation error was 23.6% at batch size 32 but 24.8% at 8, 27.3% at 4 and 34.7% at 2. Their alternative, GroupNorm, divides the channels of a single example into G groups (G = 32 by default) and normalises over each group and all spatial positions, so it never uses other examples: its error was 24.1%, 24.2%, 24.0%, 24.2% and 24.1% at batch sizes 32, 16, 8, 4 and 2 — flat. At the regular batch size of 32 it was 0.5 points worse than BatchNorm, at batch size 2 it was 10.6 points better. With G = 1 GroupNorm is LayerNorm over channels and space (the paper measured 25.3%); with G = number of channels it is InstanceNorm (28.4% in their test), which normalises each channel of each image separately and is favoured for style transfer, where an image's contrast should not affect its style.

9. Where the norm goes in a transformer block

A transformer block has two sub-layers (attention, then a feed-forward network) each wrapped in a residual connection. The original 2017 transformer applied LayerNorm after the addition (post-norm); almost all current models apply it before the sub-layer, inside the branch (pre-norm).

Xiong et al. (2020) proved with a mean-field analysis that at initialisation, for post-norm, "the expected gradients of the parameters near the output layer are large", so a large learning rate is unstable and warmup is needed, whereas for pre-norm "the gradients are well-behaved at initialization", and they trained pre-norm transformers without the warm-up stage with comparable results. Two refinements matter in current models. First, pre-norm needs a final norm after the last block (before the output projection), because the residual stream's scale has grown through depth. Second, the extra stability of putting norms after sub-layers has been revived: Gemma 2 applies RMSNorm to "the input and output of each transformer sub-layer", and OLMo 2 uses "reordered norm", h = x + RMSNorm(Attention(x)), together with QK-norm (RMSNorm on the queries and keys before their dot product, "to avoid attention logits being too large, which can lead to training loss divergence") and a z-loss (dl3). These stabilise very long or high-learning-rate runs at little cost.

10. A normaliser makes the network forgiving: a measurement

Recall the dl3 experiment: a plain 30-layer ReLU network's first-layer gradient, relative to the last layer's, was 6 with the right (He) initialisation but 10⁵ with a too-large one and 3×10⁻⁴ with a too-small one. The lab of this lesson repeats it with a LayerNorm after every linear layer. Results (ratio of gradient at layer 1 to gradient at layer 30): with weights at half the He scale, 1.2×10⁻⁸ without normalisation and 0.24 with it; at He scale, 6.2 without and 0.24 with; at four times the He scale, 1.8×10¹⁸ without and 0.24 with. The same number for an initialisation range of a factor of eight — the LayerNorm has made the gradient independent of the weight scale, exactly what the scale-invariance argument of section 4 predicts. (The exact 0.24 depends on the random draw and the depth, but the independence of the initial scale is exact.) This is why normalised networks train from careless initialisations and tolerate large learning rates.

11. Practical rules

  • ε and precision. ε ≈ 10⁻⁵ (10⁻⁶ in some models) guards the division. Compute the statistics and the division in float32 even if the rest of the model runs in bfloat16 or float16; low-precision sums of squares over thousands of features lose accuracy.
  • Weight decay. Do not apply weight decay to γ and β (and biases): decaying γ towards zero fights the normalisation. Optimiser parameter groups (dl5) handle this.
  • Initialisation. γ = 1, β = 0 at the start, so the layer initially is pure standardisation. (Gemma-style norms parameterise the scale as 1 + weight with weight initialised to 0; the checkpoint convention must be respected when porting.)
  • Fold BatchNorm for inference. Since eval-mode BatchNorm is an affine map, it merges into the preceding convolution: w′ = w·γ/√(σ² + ε), b′ = β + γ(b − μ)/√(σ² + ε). Worked with w = 2, b = 0.5, running mean 1, variance 4, γ = 1.5, β = 0.2: w′ = 1.5 and b′ = 0.2 + 1.5 × (0.5 − 1)/2 = −0.175, and (1.5x − 0.175) equals the unfused output for every x.
  • Train/eval discipline. Call model.train() and model.eval() deliberately; in fine-tuning with small batches keep BatchNorm layers in eval mode.
deep:
Scale invariance, weight norms and the effective learning rate

Suppose a layer's output goes through a normaliser, so the loss L is unchanged when the layer's weight vector w is multiplied by c > 0: L(cw) = L(w). Differentiate with respect to c at c = 1: ∇L(w) · w = 0, so the gradient is orthogonal to the weights. A gradient step therefore moves the weights along a tangent and, by Pythagoras, increases the norm: ‖w − η∇L‖² = ‖w‖² + η²‖∇L‖². So weight norms grow during training with plain gradient descent. Differentiating again shows the gradient scales inversely with the weights: ∇L(cw) = ∇L(w)/c. Together: as ‖w‖ grows, the gradient shrinks like 1/‖w‖ and the change in the direction of w per step shrinks like η/‖w‖². This is an automatic learning-rate decay, controlled by the weight norm. It explains why BatchNorm networks tolerate a large initial learning rate (the weights grow until the effective rate is stable), why it makes a huge difference whether weight decay is used (weight decay shrinks ‖w‖ and so raises the effective rate; the balance between growth from gradients and shrinkage from decay sets an equilibrium effective learning rate), and why changing weight decay changes results in normalised networks in ways it would not in a plain one. It also warns against reading a weight-norm curve naively: a growing norm in a normalised layer is expected and does not by itself indicate instability.

BatchNorm leaks information between examples

Because one example's output depends on its batch-mates, BatchNorm can leak. In contrastive self-supervised learning (dl11), the positive pair sits inside the same batch as the negatives, and the batch statistics can let a model infer which examples belong together without learning good features — the "shortcut" that MoCo avoided with shuffled BatchNorm (statistics computed on a different device split for query and key encoders) and SimCLR with a global BatchNorm across devices. At serving time, using batch statistics would make one user's response depend on other users' requests batched with theirs, which is unacceptable for privacy and reproducibility, another reason transformer inference avoids it.

Norm layers as memory-bound kernels

A LayerNorm or RMSNorm does about 5–10 arithmetic operations per element but must read the whole activation and write it back: its arithmetic intensity is far below the GPU's ridge point (gpu2), so it is bounded by memory bandwidth, and an unfused implementation that computes the mean, the variance, the normalisation and the scale as separate kernels reads and writes the tensor several times. Production stacks fuse the whole norm into one kernel (and often fuse it with the residual add and the following quantisation), computing in float32 registers but reading and writing bfloat16. torch.compile generates such fusions automatically (gpu6). RMSNorm's advantage over LayerNorm is exactly here: one fewer reduction and no bias, so a leaner kernel.

Normalisation-free approaches

If normalisation only serves to keep scales controlled and gradients well-conditioned, similar effects may be obtained differently. NFNets (Brock et al., 2021) train large-batch ResNets without BatchNorm by scaling weights (scaled weight standardisation) and using adaptive gradient clipping — clipping each unit's gradient by the ratio of its norm to its weight's norm — and matched or surpassed BatchNorm models on ImageNet. Zhu et al. (2025) observed that trained LayerNorms in transformers often produce a tanh-like S-shaped input–output mapping and proposed Dynamic Tanh, tanh(αx) with a learnable scalar α, as a drop-in replacement; they report comparable results across vision and language models. Neither has displaced normalisation as the default, but they clarify what the layer is doing: bounding and re-scaling activations elementwise in a way that keeps optimisation well-behaved.

Conditioning: adaptive normalisation

The learned γ and β need not be fixed parameters; they can be predicted from other data. In conditional image generation (dl10), adaptive layer norm (adaLN, used in diffusion transformers) computes γ and β from the conditioning signal (the diffusion timestep, a class label), so a single network can behave differently per condition, and in style transfer AdaIN sets the per-channel statistics from a style image. This shows that after standardisation, γ and β are the natural place to inject information: the standardised activations are "content", and the affine parameters set their scale and offset.

Batch size, BatchNorm and the effective batch

With data parallelism, per-GPU batch size determines BatchNorm's statistics quality, so scaling out a fixed global batch over more GPUs shrinks the per-GPU batch and can degrade BatchNorm models even though the global batch is unchanged — a subtle scale-out bug. Goyal et al.'s ImageNet-in-an-hour work (ml4) kept the per-GPU batch at 32 and computed BatchNorm statistics per GPU, so that the definition of the loss did not depend on the number of GPUs. The alternatives are SyncBatchNorm (exact global statistics, one all-reduce of sums per norm layer per pass), 'ghost' batch normalisation (deliberately computing statistics over small virtual sub-batches as a regulariser) or replacing the norm with GroupNorm. The same reasoning is why gradient accumulation does not reproduce a large batch for BatchNorm networks: each micro-batch's statistics are computed alone (dl1).

Failure at the edge: ε, zeros and outliers

If a feature is (nearly) constant across the pooled set, its variance is close to zero and the output is dominated by ε: with ε = 10⁻⁵ and variance 10⁻⁶, the standard deviation is 0.0033 rather than 0.001, and tiny noise can be amplified by a factor of 300. In float16, x² can overflow above 256 in magnitude (256² = 65,536 > 65,504) if the sum of squares is computed in half precision, another reason for float32 accumulation. In LLMs a few hidden dimensions develop very large magnitudes ("massive activations" or outlier features); RMSNorm divides everything by an RMS dominated by those dimensions, which shrinks the informative ones — an interaction that motivates some of the quantisation and architecture work around outliers (dl2, gpu4).
prod:
The public case: Batch Normalization on Inception

Ioffe and Szegedy's paper (arXiv:1502.03167, Google, 2015) is short and dense with checkable numbers. They took the Inception network (batch size 32, learning rate 0.0015, momentum SGD), which reached 72.2% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet validation set after 31 × 10⁶ steps, and inserted BatchNorm before each non-linearity. Their results, from the paper's Figure 3: BN-Baseline (BatchNorm only) reached 72.2% in 13.3 million steps — less than half; BN-x5 (also with a 5× higher learning rate, 0.0075, plus modifications such as removing dropout and reducing L2 weight regularisation by 5×) reached it in 2.1 million steps, the "14 times fewer steps" of the abstract, with a maximum accuracy of 73.0%; BN-x30 (learning rate 0.045, thirty times the original) trained "somewhat slower initially" but reached 74.8%, the best single-network accuracy, in about 6 million steps. Applying the same 5× learning rate to the original Inception "caused the model parameters to reach machine infinity". BN-x5-Sigmoid, the same network with sigmoid non-linearities, reached 69.8%, while "without Batch Normalization, Inception with sigmoid never achieves better than 1/1000 accuracy" — chance. An ensemble of six BN-x30-based networks achieved 4.9% top-5 validation error and 4.82% test error, ahead of the previous best of 4.94% (He et al.'s PReLU ensemble, dl2) and, the authors note, better than the estimated accuracy of human raters. The lessons are the ones from this lesson: normalisation buys a much larger usable learning rate (5× to 30×), makes training insensitive to activation choice (sigmoid works), and acts as a regulariser (dropout could be reduced or removed).

The counterpart case is Wu and He's Group Normalization paper (arXiv:1803.08494, Facebook AI Research, 2018), which quantified BatchNorm's weakness: ResNet-50's ImageNet error rose from 23.6% (batch 32) to 34.7% (batch 2), while GroupNorm with 32 groups was flat at 24.0–24.2%. For detection and segmentation (Mask R-CNN on COCO), where per-GPU batches are 1–2 images, they found that GroupNorm improved over the standard workaround of freezing BatchNorm into a fixed affine layer (their BN* baseline) by 1.1 box AP and 0.8 mask AP.

Real-world incident classes

The model that is great in training and poor in production. The number-one cause is a missing model.eval(), or running inference under model.train() with a small batch. Symptoms: accuracy that changes with batch size or with the order of requests, and predictions that are not deterministic. A one-line assertion at service start-up (assert not model.training) prevents it; a test that feeds the same example alone and inside a batch and checks that outputs match to within numerical noise detects any remaining batch dependence.

Silent drift of running statistics in fine-tuning. After a few hundred steps of fine-tuning with batch size 2–4, evaluation accuracy is far worse than at start although the training loss falls. The running mean and variance have been overwritten by noisy small-batch estimates. Fix by freezing BatchNorm (eval mode for those layers), or by using GroupNorm, and always compare against the pretrained statistics.

Porting bugs in norm layers. The Gemma port story in dl2 is also a norm story: the community fix (Hugging Face transformers PR #29402) listed, alongside the approximate GELU, that the RMSNorm which multiplies by (1 + weight) "must be upcasted to float32 and not bfloat16 or float16 halfway", unlike LLaMA's version, which downcasts before multiplying by the weights. Differences of this kind (ε, upcasting order, weight convention, whether the mean is subtracted) produce small numerical drift that grows with depth. A layer-by-layer comparison against a reference implementation on fixed inputs finds the first layer that diverges.

Instability that norm placement can cure. Loss spikes in long high-learning-rate runs are often attention logits growing (dl3). OLMo 2's technical report lists RMSNorm, reordered norm (normalising sub-layer outputs), QK-norm and z-loss among the stability measures it adopted; Gemma 2 normalises the input and output of every sub-layer. If a run is spiking, adding QK-norm or output norms is a cheaper experiment than changing the optimiser.

What to monitor

For BatchNorm networks: the running mean and variance of each layer over time (a running variance collapsing towards zero or a running mean far from the training data's indicates a problem), the difference in accuracy between train and eval modes on the same held-out data, and per-GPU batch size. For LayerNorm and RMSNorm models: activation RMS at the input of each block (it should grow smoothly with depth in pre-norm models, and a sudden jump points at a layer), the γ statistics (a γ growing without bound or collapsing to zero in one layer), and gradient norms per layer (dl3). During porting or quantisation: layer-wise output error against a float32 reference.
myths: BatchNorm works because it removes "internal covariate shift".

That was the original motivation, and it is the explanation in the 2015 paper's title, but Santurkar et al. (2018) showed that adding random noise after each BatchNorm layer, which deliberately reintroduces covariate shift, barely hurt training. Their account is that BatchNorm makes the loss landscape smoother, so gradients are more predictive and larger learning rates are safe. The debate is not fully closed, but "it stops the distribution shifting" is no longer the accepted answer.
LayerNorm is just BatchNorm applied along a different axis, so they behave the same.

The axis is the whole difference in behaviour. BatchNorm's statistics depend on the other examples in the batch, so it has a training mode and an evaluation mode (running averages), degrades with tiny batches (ResNet-50 error 23.6% at batch 32 rising to 34.7% at batch 2 in Wu & He's test), and is awkward with padded sequences. LayerNorm's statistics come from one example only, so it behaves identically in training and inference, at any batch size and any sequence length.
Normalising to zero mean and unit variance limits what the network can represent.

Every normalisation layer is followed by a learned scale γ and shift β per feature, so the layer can represent the identity (γ = std, β = mean) or any other scaling. Normalisation changes how the function is parameterised — decoupling each layer's output scale from the weights below it — without reducing what it can express.
RMSNorm is a cheap approximation that loses quality compared with LayerNorm.

RMSNorm keeps the property that seems to matter — invariance to the scale of the input — and drops the mean subtraction and the bias. Zhang & Sennrich found comparable quality with 7–64% less running time depending on the model, and LLaMA, Gemma and OLMo 2 all use it. It is not an approximation in the lossy sense; it is a different, simpler layer that works as well.
Normalisation layers only matter for training, so you can ignore them at inference.

BatchNorm at inference is a different function from BatchNorm in training (it uses stored running statistics), and forgetting model.eval() is one of the most common reasons a model that trained well predicts badly. Even LayerNorm and RMSNorm matter at inference: their epsilon, float32 upcasting and (1 + weight) conventions have to match the checkpoint, or outputs drift.
Pre-norm and post-norm are equivalent; it is a style choice.

Xiong et al. showed that in the original post-norm transformer the expected gradients near the output layer are large at initialisation, so training needs learning-rate warmup, while pre-norm gradients are well-behaved. Pre-norm keeps a clean identity path along the residual stream, which is why most LLMs use it; the cost is that the residual stream's magnitude grows with depth, and some recent models add extra norms after the sub-layers.
lab:
Goal: implement the three normalisers on the lesson's 2×3 tensor, show their different dependence on the batch, verify the LayerNorm gradient formula against finite differences, see BatchNorm's running statistics, and repeat the dl3 experiment to watch a normaliser make a 30-layer network insensitive to initialisation. NumPy only, Python 3.12, a few seconds.

import numpy as np
EPS = 1e-5

# ---- three normalisers; x has shape (batch, features)
def batchnorm(x):  m, v = x.mean(0), x.var(0);                 return (x - m) / np.sqrt(v + EPS)
def layernorm(x):  m, v = x.mean(1, keepdims=True), x.var(1, keepdims=True); return (x - m) / np.sqrt(v + EPS)
def rmsnorm(x):    return x / np.sqrt((x ** 2).mean(1, keepdims=True) + EPS)

X = np.array([[2., 4., 6.], [0., 3., 9.]])
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)
print("BatchNorm (per column):\n", batchnorm(X))
print("LayerNorm (per row):\n", layernorm(X))
print("RMSNorm (per row):\n", rmsnorm(X))

# ---- batch dependence: change the OTHER example, look at example 0's output
X2 = X.copy(); X2[1] = [100., 200., 300.]
print("\nexample 0 after swapping its batch-mate:  BN", batchnorm(X2)[0], " LN", layernorm(X2)[0])

# ---- train-mode BatchNorm with a batch of one destroys the input (mean = the value, variance = 0)
print("BN, batch of 1:", batchnorm(np.array([[2., 4., 6.]])))

# ---- LayerNorm backward by formula vs finite differences
def ln_backward(dy, x):
    xh, s = layernorm(x), np.sqrt(x.var(1, keepdims=True) + EPS)
    return (dy - dy.mean(1, keepdims=True) - xh * (dy * xh).mean(1, keepdims=True)) / s
x = np.array([[2., 4., 6.]]); dy = np.array([[1., 0., 0.]])
num = np.zeros_like(x)
for j in range(3):
    e = np.zeros_like(x); e[0, j] = 1e-6
    num[0, j] = ((layernorm(x + e) - layernorm(x - e)) * dy).sum() / 2e-6
print("\nLN backward  formula:", ln_backward(dy, x), " finite differences:", num)
print("gradient along the normalised direction is removed:", ln_backward(-layernorm(x), x))

# ---- running statistics for BatchNorm (momentum 0.1): what eval mode would use
batch = np.array([2., 4., 6., 8.]); rm, rv = 0.0, 1.0
rm, rv = 0.9 * rm + 0.1 * batch.mean(), 0.9 * rv + 0.1 * batch.var(ddof=1)
print("\nafter one batch: running mean", rm, " running var", round(rv, 3))

# ---- does a normaliser rescue a badly scaled 30-layer network? (compare dl3)
DEPTH, WIDTH = 30, 100
def signal(std, norm, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Ws = [r.normal(0, std, (WIDTH, WIDTH)) for _ in range(DEPTH)]
    h, cache = r.normal(size=(64, WIDTH)), []
    for W in Ws:
        z = h @ W
        y = layernorm(z) if norm else z
        a = np.maximum(y, 0)
        cache.append((z, y)); h = a
    d = np.ones_like(h) / h.size; out = []
    for W, (z, y) in zip(reversed(Ws), reversed(cache)):
        dy = d * (y > 0)
        dz = ln_backward(dy, z) if norm else dy
        d = dz @ W.T; out.append(np.linalg.norm(d))
    return out[-1] / out[0]                          # gradient at layer 1 relative to the top
print("\ngradient at layer 1 / gradient at layer 30, ReLU, 30 layers")
for label, std in [("too small (0.5x He)", 0.5 * np.sqrt(2 / WIDTH)), ("He", np.sqrt(2 / WIDTH)), ("too big (4x He)", 4 * np.sqrt(2 / WIDTH))]:
    print(f"{label:20} no norm {signal(std, False):9.1e}   with LayerNorm {signal(std, True):9.1e}")

What to look for.

  1. The three tables match section 2: BatchNorm gives [[1, 1, −1], [−1, −1, 1]] (a batch of two can only produce ±1); LayerNorm gives row 1 = (−1.225, 0, 1.225) and row 2 = (−1.069, −0.267, 1.336); RMSNorm gives (0.463, 0.926, 1.389) and (0, 0.548, 1.643).
  2. Batch dependence. After replacing example 1 with (100, 200, 300), example 0's LayerNorm output is unchanged but its BatchNorm output flips from (1, 1, −1) to (−1, −1, −1). This is the difference in one line.
  3. Batch of one. Train-mode BatchNorm returns all zeros (β) for a single example: the batch mean is the value itself and the variance is zero.
  4. The gradient formula agrees with finite differences: (0.102, −0.204, 0.102), and a gradient along the normalised direction comes out as zero — scale invariance made visible.
  5. Running statistics. After one batch (2, 4, 6, 8) with momentum 0.1 the running mean is 0.5 and the running variance 1.567.
  6. The depth experiment prints the gradient ratio (layer 1 ÷ layer 30) for three weight scales. Without normalisation it swings from about 10⁻⁸ through 6 to about 10¹⁸; with LayerNorm it is 0.24 in all three rows. Try depth 60, or remove the ReLU, and see that the invariance to the initial weight scale persists.

Try next. Add γ and β and write their gradients (dγ = Σ dy ⊙ x̂, dβ = Σ dy); implement BatchNorm's backward and check it the same way; implement GroupNorm with a group count G and confirm that G = 1 reproduces LayerNorm over the same axes and G = features reproduces InstanceNorm.
recap: A normalisation layer subtracts a mean and divides by a standard deviation computed over some set of activations, then applies a learned per-feature scale γ and shift β; the only difference between the variants is which set of activations shares one mean and variance.

BatchNorm pools over the batch (and spatial positions) for each channel; LayerNorm pools over the features of each single example (and token); RMSNorm is LayerNorm without the mean subtraction and bias, dividing only by the root-mean-square.

On the 2×3 tensor [[2,4,6],[0,3,9]], LayerNorm turns row 1 into (−1.22, 0, 1.22) and RMSNorm into (0.46, 0.93, 1.39), while BatchNorm over a batch of two can only output ±1 in every column — an extreme illustration of why BatchNorm needs reasonable batch sizes.

BatchNorm uses batch statistics in training and stored running averages (momentum 0.1) at inference, so eval mode is mandatory, batch size 1 in training mode outputs β for every input, and domain shift or tiny fine-tuning batches corrupt the running statistics.

Normalisation makes a layer invariant to the scale of its input, so gradients no longer depend on the scale of the weights below; in the lab a 30-layer network's first-to-last gradient ratio was 0.24 for initialisations that ranged over a factor of eight, without normalisation it ranged from 10⁻⁸ to 10¹⁸.

BatchNorm let Inception match its baseline accuracy with 14× fewer steps (Ioffe & Szegedy), and its benefit is best explained by a smoother loss landscape and scale invariance rather than by removing covariate shift.

Transformers use LayerNorm or RMSNorm because they are batch-independent, identical in training and inference and indifferent to padding; modern LLMs use RMSNorm in a pre-norm arrangement, with a final norm before the output head, sometimes QK-norm and extra post-sub-layer norms.

GroupNorm (groups of channels within one example) gives BatchNorm-like accuracy without a batch dependency: on ResNet-50 its error stayed at 24.0–24.2% for batch sizes 32 down to 2 while BatchNorm rose from 23.6% to 34.7%.

Practical rules: keep norm computations in float32, exclude γ and β from weight decay, match ε and the weight convention when porting checkpoints, and fold BatchNorm into the preceding convolution for inference.
glossary: The learned per-feature scale γ and shift β applied after normalising; they let the layer represent any scale and offset.
