Read it: the cell kept 90% of its old memory (f = 0.905) and wrote 0.785 of new content (i·g). The backward pass through this step shows the design at work. The derivative of the new cell with respect to the old one is exactly ∂c_t/∂c_(t−1) = f = 0.905, a single gate value — no weight matrix, no squashing slope. The gradient over the next T steps along the cell path is the product of the forget gates: with f ≈ 0.95 constant it is 0.95⁵⁰ = 0.077 after 50 steps, with f ≈ 0.99 it is 0.605, with f ≈ 0.999 it is 0.951, whereas a plain RNN with per-step factor 0.7 has 10⁻⁸ after 50 steps. The network can learn to push f toward 1 for information it needs to keep. The lab verifies the gate values, and PyTorch's LSTMCell computes the same thing (its gate order is input, forget, candidate, output).

What this buys, and what it does not. The lab's measurement is the honest picture: an LSTM with a forget-gate bias of 1 still lost a factor of 10⁻⁸ over 50 steps, only better than the plain RNN's 10⁻²². The architecture makes long memory possible and learnable: gate biases can be pushed high, the network can learn f near 1 where memory is needed, and the gradient along the cell path survives. It does not make memory automatic. Initialising the forget-gate bias to a positive value (1 or more; Gers et al. 2000 and Jozefowicz et al. 2015 report it matters) starts the cell in "remember by default" mode, since a bias of 0 gives f = 0.5 and halves the memory each step. Tallec and Ollivier's "chrono initialisation" goes further and sets forget biases so that units cover a spread of time scales matching the expected dependency lengths.

History and variants. The 1997 LSTM had input and output gates but no forget gate: the carousel simply kept everything, which makes it hard to reset. Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins (2000) added the forget gate. Peephole connections let gates see the cell state; coupled input–forget gates set i = 1 − f. Greff et al. ("LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey") ablated the variants and found none clearly better than the standard cell, with the forget gate and output activation function the most important parts.

Size. Each of the four blocks has an input matrix, a recurrent matrix and a bias, so an LSTM layer has 4·(n(m + n) + n) parameters: for m = 300 and n = 512, 4 × 416,256 = 1,665,024 (PyTorch, which stores two bias vectors per block, reports 1,667,072 — the lab checks against the library when it is installed). It is four times a plain RNN's parameter count and roughly four times its computation per step.

6. The GRU

Cho et al. (2014) proposed the gated recurrent unit, a simplification of the LSTM with no separate cell state and two gates:

z_t = σ( W_z x_t + U_z h_(t−1) + b_z )              update gate — how much to move toward the new candidate
r_t = σ( W_r x_t + U_r h_(t−1) + b_r )              reset gate  — how much of the old state feeds the candidate
h̃_t = tanh( W x_t + U (r_t ⊙ h_(t−1)) + b )         candidate state
h_t = (1 − z_t) ⊙ h_(t−1) + z_t ⊙ h̃_t              interpolate between old state and candidate

(Conventions differ: Cho et al. and PyTorch define z as the keep gate, h_t = z ⊙ h_(t−1) + (1 − z) ⊙ h̃_t; the two are the same model with z ↔ 1 − z.) The last line is the GRU's additive path: when z_t is near 0 the state is copied unchanged, so gradients pass with gain 1 − z_t, the same idea as the LSTM's forget gate (here the forget and input gates are tied: keep the fraction 1 − z of the old, write z of the new). It has three weight blocks instead of four (1,248,768 parameters at m = 300, n = 512 versus 1,665,024) and one state vector instead of two. Chung et al. (2014) compared LSTM and GRU on music and speech modelling and found both clearly better than plain tanh units and roughly comparable to each other. In practice LSTMs are the default when in doubt and GRUs are chosen for speed and size.

7. Architectures built from recurrent cells

  • Stacked RNNs: the hidden-state sequence of layer 1 is the input sequence of layer 2. Depth adds capacity; Sutskever et al. found four-layer LSTMs clearly better than shallow ones. Residual connections between layers (GNMT) allow eight or more.
  • Bidirectional RNNs: one RNN reads left to right, another right to left, and their states are concatenated at each position, so every position sees its whole context. Right for tagging, classification and encoders; impossible for generation (the future does not exist).
  • Encoder–decoder (seq2seq): the encoder's final state initialises the decoder, which generates the output one token at a time, feeding back its own previous output.
  • Teacher forcing. During training the decoder is fed the true previous token, not its own prediction; this stabilises and parallelises training but creates exposure bias: at inference the decoder consumes its own (possibly wrong) tokens, a situation it never saw. Scheduled sampling mixes the two.
  • Decoding. Greedy decoding picks the top token at each step; beam search keeps the k best partial sequences (Sutskever et al. found a beam of just 2 captured most of the benefit; they used 12 for their headline result), typically with a length normalisation so that short outputs are not favoured.

8. The fixed-vector bottleneck and attention

In the basic encoder–decoder the encoder must compress the entire source sentence into one vector, the final hidden state, from which the decoder generates everything. A fixed-size vector has fixed capacity, so quality degrades on long sentences. Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2014) "conjecture that the use of a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck" and propose to let the decoder look back at all of the encoder's states and choose. At each output step i the decoder computes a score between its current state and each encoder state h_j, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and takes the weighted sum as that step's context:

e_ij = score(s_(i−1), h_j)          α_ij = softmax_j(e_ij)          c_i = Σ_j α_ij · h_j

Worked example. Three encoder states h₁ = (1, 0), h₂ = (0, 1), h₃ = (1, 1). At some decoder step the scores are (2.0, 1.0, 0.1). Exponentials: 7.389, 2.718, 1.105, summing to 11.213, so the weights are α = (0.659, 0.242, 0.099) (the same numbers as the softmax in dl1). The context is c = 0.659·(1, 0) + 0.242·(0, 1) + 0.099·(1, 1) = (0.758, 0.341): dominated by the encoder state the decoder found most relevant. Nothing is compressed: at every step the decoder can pick a different mixture.

9. Why recurrent models lost, and what remains

Two structural limits, both visible in the numbers, ended the RNN era for large models.

  1. No parallelism over time. The state at step t needs the state at step t−1, in both the forward and the backward pass. A 2,048-token sequence is a chain of 2,048 dependent matrix multiplications, each small (batch × n by n × 4n), so a GPU with tens of thousands of cores sits mostly idle. A transformer computes all 2,048 positions in a handful of large matrix multiplies, with a causal mask enforcing order. That difference in hardware utilisation, more than any difference in modelling power, is why transformers scaled to trillions of tokens.
  2. Limited effective memory. Even a well-trained LSTM does not use its whole history. Khandelwal et al. (2018), "Sharp Nearby, Fuzzy Far Away", measured LSTM language models and found they use "about 200 tokens of context on average", with word order mattering only for the nearest ~50 tokens. And a fixed-size state cannot store an arbitrary earlier token exactly: exact copying and recall are hard, while attention can look back at any position directly.

The attention-versus-recurrence trade at inference is easy to state with numbers. A 7-billion-parameter transformer (32 layers, width 4,096, bf16) keeps a KV cache of 2 (keys and values) × 32 × 4,096 × 2 bytes = 0.5 MB per token (gpu3); at 4,096 tokens that is 2 GB per sequence. A recurrent model of the same width and depth keeps an LSTM state of 2 (h and c) × 32 × 4,096 × 2 bytes = 0.5 MB in total, whatever the context length: one token of transformer cache equals the entire recurrent state. That constant memory and constant per-token cost is why recurrent ideas keep coming back.

deep:
Why the LSTM's gradient is only partly protected

Differentiate the LSTM step and the state Jacobian has two parts. Along the cell state, ∂c_t/∂c_(t−1) = diag(f_t), plus terms that arrive through the gates' dependence on h_(t−1) (each gate is a function of h_(t−1), and h_(t−1) depends on c_(t−1) through o ⊙ tanh(c)). The first term is the protected carousel: it has no weight matrix and no squashing slope. The second contains the usual products of weight matrices and slopes and can vanish or explode like a plain RNN's. Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's paper acknowledged this by truncating the gradient at the gates in the original algorithm ("truncating the gradient where this does not do harm"), so that error flows through the carousel only and not around the recurrent connections. Modern implementations use full BPTT, but the picture stands: the guaranteed part of the gradient is the cell-state path, whose gain is the product of forget gates, and long-range learning succeeds when the network drives those gates to 1. Corollaries: gate saturation near 1 is desired for memory cells and a symptom of a problem for forgetting ones; initial forget-gate biases set the initial time scale of memory (a gate value f corresponds to a time constant of 1/(1 − f) steps: 0.73 gives about 4 steps, 0.99 gives 100); and layer normalisation applied inside the cell stabilises the gate pre-activations.

Regularisation and optimisation of LSTM language models

Before transformers, the best language models were heavily regularised LSTMs. Merity, Keskar and Socher's AWD-LSTM (2017) is the canonical recipe: weight-dropped recurrent connections (DropConnect on the hidden-to-hidden matrices), variational dropout (the same dropout mask at every time step within a sequence, rather than fresh noise each step, which would erase memory), embedding dropout, weight tying between input embedding and output softmax, ASGD optimisation, and truncated BPTT with randomised sequence lengths. The same architecture was the base of ULMFiT (dl11), the first widely used pretrain-then-fine-tune recipe for text. The lesson in variational dropout is worth remembering for interviews: ordinary dropout applied independently at each step destroys the recurrent signal, because a memory unit dropped at step 7 loses what it carried from step 6; tying the mask across steps preserves it.

Parallelising a linear recurrence: the scan and the convolution views

The LSTM and GRU are non-linear in h: the gates depend on h_(t−1), so step t genuinely needs step t−1. Take that dependency away and something remarkable happens. A linear recurrence h_t = a_t·h_(t−1) + b_t is a composition of affine maps, and composing two of them gives another: applying (a₁, b₁) then (a₂, b₂) equals the single map (a₂·a₁, a₂·b₁ + b₂). Because that composition is associative, all T states can be computed with a parallel prefix scan in about log₂ T rounds of fully parallel work, instead of T dependent steps. The lab does this for T = 8: 3 rounds instead of 8, with identical results. When a and b do not depend on the position (a fixed linear system), the whole recurrence is a convolution: y_t = Σ_k c·a^k·b·u_(t−k) is convolution of the input with the kernel (c·b, c·a·b, c·a²·b, …). For a = 0.9, b = c = 1 the kernel is (1, 0.9, 0.81, 0.729, …), exactly a geometrically decaying memory, and it can be applied with an FFT in O(T log T), or by the sliding windows of dl6 (a long convolution). So a linear recurrent model has three equivalent forms: a recurrence (O(1) memory per step at inference), a convolution (parallel training), and a scan (parallel training with input-dependent parameters).

State-space models. S4 (Gu et al., 2021) parameterises a continuous-time linear system x′(t) = A x(t) + B u(t), y(t) = C x(t), discretises it to h_t = Ā h_(t−1) + B̄ u_t, and uses a special structured initialisation of A (HiPPO) so the state approximates a running summary of the whole history; it trains as a long convolution and runs as a recurrence. Its weakness is that A, B, C are fixed: the model cannot choose what to remember based on content, which hurts language. Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) makes B, C and the step size input-dependent ("selective"), which gives content-based forgetting and writing like an LSTM's gates but in a linear-in-state form, and computes it with a hardware-aware parallel scan (fusing the recurrence into GPU registers and shared memory rather than materialising the expanded state, gpu6). The paper reports 5× higher inference throughput than transformers, linear scaling in sequence length, and Mamba-3B matching transformers twice its size on language modelling. RWKV is a related architecture, trained in parallel like a transformer and run as an RNN. Linear attention (Katharopoulos et al., 2020, "Transformers are RNNs") replaces the softmax with a feature-map kernel so that causal attention becomes S_t = S_(t−1) + φ(k_t) v_tᵀ, y_t = S_tᵀ φ(q_t): an RNN whose state is a matrix. Hybrids interleaving a few attention layers with state-space layers try to keep exact recall where it matters while keeping most layers at constant memory.

The fixed-size state and what it cannot do

A recurrent state of n numbers can carry at most about n·(bits per number) of information about the past, however long the context. Tasks that require exact reproduction of an arbitrary earlier span (copying a long string, looking up a key–value pair mentioned 10,000 tokens ago) need capacity proportional to the context, which an attention layer gets for free because it stores the entire history in the KV cache. Empirical work on recurrent and state-space models finds them weaker than transformers on such recall and copying tasks at matched size, and stronger on cost. That is the trade behind hybrids (a small fraction of attention layers to a majority of recurrent ones) and the reason "transformers are RNNs with a state that grows with the sequence" is a useful way of seeing the whole family.

Training tricks worth knowing

Truncated BPTT with state carry-over: keep hidden states across consecutive chunks of a long document (stateful training) but detach them (h = h.detach()) so the graph does not grow; reset at document boundaries. Gradient clipping at a global norm around 0.25–5 is standard for recurrent nets (Pascanu et al.). Layer normalisation inside the cell (dl4) stabilises training and is used in many recurrent architectures. cuDNN fuses the four gate matmuls into one and pipelines layers and time steps (the wavefront of layer l at step t can overlap with layer l+1 at step t−1), recovering some parallelism from a stacked recurrence. Packed sequences avoid computing on padding. Connectionist temporal classification (CTC) and RNN transducers extend recurrent models to speech and handwriting where input and output lengths differ and alignment is unknown, and streaming RNN-transducer models remain common for on-device speech recognition because their state is small and their latency constant.
prod:
The public case: LSTM (1997), sequence-to-sequence (2014), GNMT (2016)

Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber's "Long Short-Term Memory" (Neural Computation 9(8), 1997) is a long paper (46 pages) whose abstract makes its claims plain: recurrent learning "takes a very long time, mostly due to insufficient, decaying error backflow"; LSTM, by "enforcing constant error flow through constant error carrousels within special units" with multiplicative gate units that "learn to open and close access to the constant error flow", "can learn to bridge minimal time lags in excess of 1000 discrete time steps"; it is "local in space and time; its computational complexity per time step and weight is O(1)"; and, on artificial long-time-lag tasks, it "leads to many more successful runs, and learns much faster" than real-time recurrent learning, BPTT and other methods, and "solves complex, artificial long time lag tasks that have never been solved by previous recurrent network algorithms". Note what it is: a 1997 result on synthetic benchmarks. It took a further 17 years for hardware and data to make LSTMs a mainstream tool.

The moment it became one is Sutskever, Vinyals and Le's "Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks" (2014). A four-layer LSTM encoder read the English sentence into a vector; a four-layer LSTM decoder produced the French. Vocabularies were 160,000 source and 80,000 target words, the state dimension was 1,000 per layer, and each model had about 384 million parameters (as a check: eight LSTM layers of 8 million each is 64M, the two embedding tables 160M + 80M, and the output softmax 80M, summing to 384M); the headline result is an ensemble of five such models. On the WMT'14 English–French test set the ensemble reached a BLEU score of 34.81, "by far the best result achieved by direct translation with large neural networks", compared with 33.30 for the phrase-based statistical baseline. A striking detail: reversing the order of the words in the source sentences (not the targets) "improved the LSTM's performance markedly", because it put the first source words next to the first target words and created many short-range dependencies that made optimisation easier; the authors call it "one of the key technical contributions of this work". The same fixed-vector design also exposed the bottleneck: Bahdanau et al. (2014) replaced it with attention and on English–French with sentences of up to 50 words measured 26.75 BLEU (RNNsearch-50) against 17.82 for the fixed-vector RNNencdec-50 on the full test set, and, unlike the fixed-vector model, RNNsearch did not degrade with sentence length.

Two years later Google's Neural Machine Translation system (Wu et al., 2016) put the design into production: an LSTM encoder–decoder with 8 encoder layers (the first bidirectional) and 8 decoder layers, residual connections between layers and attention from decoder to encoder. In a human side-by-side evaluation on simple sentences it "reduces translation errors by an average of 60% compared to Google's phrase-based production system" across several language pairs. It is the high-water mark of LSTM machine translation; the transformer paper appeared the following year and the recurrent encoder–decoder was displaced.

Failure modes and debugging

State leaking between sequences. A stateful LSTM that carries its hidden state across batches (correct for consecutive chunks of one long document) but is fed unrelated sequences, or is not reset at document boundaries, conditions each example on the previous one: validation loss looks fine within a document and evaluation on shuffled data is worse. Reset explicitly, and for independent sequences start from zero states.

Padding and masking errors. Averaging the loss over padded positions dilutes it and teaches the model to predict padding; letting padding tokens update the state of a finished sequence changes its final state (which is then used for classification). Use packed sequences or masks in both the loss and the recurrence, and test with a batch where one sequence is padded versus alone: outputs must match.

Memory blow-up from BPTT. Not detaching the carried state makes the autograd graph span the whole dataset: memory grows every batch until out of memory (dl1). BPTT also stores activations at every step: for a layer of width 1,024, batch 64 and 2,048 steps that is about 3 GB per layer. Truncate, checkpoint, or shrink.

Exploding gradients and NaNs. Loss spikes and NaNs in recurrent nets are usually exploding gradients; clip the global norm (values of 0.25–5 are typical), lower the learning rate, and check that forget-gate biases are not so large that the cell saturates and blows up.

Exposure bias and decoding surprises. A model that is excellent under teacher forcing may produce repetitive or derailed text under free running; evaluate with the same decoding you will deploy, and try beam search with length normalisation (beam search without normalisation prefers short outputs) or scheduled sampling.

A bidirectional layer in a generator. Sees the future during training; validation loss is impossibly good and inference collapses. Bidirectionality belongs only in encoders and taggers.

Slow training. RNN training is latency-bound: profile before scaling up. Use cuDNN-backed implementations (in PyTorch nn.LSTM, not a Python loop over LSTMCell), larger batches, mixed precision, and a channels of parallelism from batch and layers, and consider a transformer or convolutional alternative if throughput dominates.

What to monitor

Gradient norm per step (clipping engaged?), the mean and saturation fraction of each gate (a forget gate stuck near 0 means the cell never remembers; near 1 for every unit means it never forgets), per-time-step loss (does the loss on late tokens of a long sequence keep improving with context?), the loss as a function of context length (the Khandelwal shuffle test), and for encoder–decoders the alignment map: attention weights should look like a mostly diagonal band for translation. Sudden loss spikes on a specific length bucket usually point to a batching or masking bug.
myths: LSTMs completely solve the vanishing-gradient problem.

They protect one path: the cell state, whose update c_t = f_t ⊙ c_(t−1) + i_t ⊙ g_t gives a gradient factor equal to the forget gate f_t, which the network can learn to hold near 1. In a lab measurement the LSTM's gradient gain fell to 10⁻⁸ after 50 steps with a forget-gate bias of 1 (gate ≈ 0.73), against 10⁻²² for a plain RNN, and stayed near 1.4 for 100 steps with a bias of 5. The mechanism makes long memory learnable, not automatic, and even so measured LSTM language models use only about 200 tokens of context.
Transformers replaced RNNs because attention models long-range dependencies better than LSTMs can in principle.

The decisive reason was engineering: an RNN's step t needs step t−1, so training cannot use a GPU's parallel width, while a transformer processes all positions at once. Attention was first added to RNN encoder–decoders (Bahdanau et al.) to remove the fixed-size bottleneck; the transformer then observed that with attention the recurrence was redundant. Throughput, not expressiveness, is why transformers scaled and RNNs did not.
A transformer generates tokens in parallel, unlike an RNN, so it is faster at inference.

Generation is sequential for both: each token must be chosen before the next can be produced. The transformer's parallelism is at training time (all target positions are known, with a causal mask). At inference the transformer has to attend over a KV cache that grows with context (about 0.5 MB per token for a 7B model), while a recurrent model updates a fixed-size state; that inference advantage is one reason recurrent designs are returning.
The forget gate decides what to forget, so its bias should start at 0.

Initialising the forget-gate bias to a positive value (1 or more) is a standard trick, because at initialisation f = σ(0) = 0.5 would halve the memory at every step and the cell would forget everything within a handful of steps. A positive bias starts the cell in 'remember by default' mode; in the lab, biases of 1 and 5 gave a per-step retention of about 0.73 and 0.99.
Bidirectional RNNs are a good choice for text generation.

A bidirectional RNN reads the sequence forwards and backwards, so each output depends on the whole sequence, including the future. That is right for tagging, classification and the encoder of a translation system, and impossible for generating text left to right, where the future does not exist yet. Using one in a generator leaks the answer during training and fails at inference.
GRUs are just a worse LSTM.

A GRU merges the forget and input gates into one update gate and drops the separate cell state, giving three weight blocks instead of four (1.25 million versus 1.67 million parameters at input 300 and hidden 512). Chung et al. found LSTM and GRU comparable on their tasks, both better than plain tanh units; which wins depends on the data and tuning, and the GRU is faster and smaller.
lab:
Goal: reproduce the lesson's one-step LSTM computation, measure how much gradient survives T steps in a plain RNN versus LSTMs with different forget-gate biases, see a linear recurrence computed in parallel with a prefix scan and as a convolution, and compute an attention context vector. NumPy only, Python 3.12; the parameter-count check against PyTorch runs only if torch is installed. The gradient experiment uses numerical Jacobians and takes a few seconds.

import numpy as np
sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# ---- 1. one LSTM step by hand: one input, one hidden unit (gate order i, f, g, o as in PyTorch)
def lstm_step(x, h, c, W, U, b):
    n = h.size
    z = W @ x + U @ h + b
    i, f, g, o = sig(z[:n]), sig(z[n:2 * n]), np.tanh(z[2 * n:3 * n]), sig(z[3 * n:])
    c2 = f * c + i * g                      # additive memory update: the constant-error path
    h2 = o * np.tanh(c2)
    return h2, c2, (i, f, g, o)
W = np.array([[0.6], [0.5], [1.0], [0.7]]); U = np.array([[0.4], [0.5], [0.5], [0.3]]); b = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0])
h, c, gates = lstm_step(np.array([2.0]), np.array([0.5]), np.array([1.0]), W, U, b)
print("gates i, f, g, o =", np.round([float(v[0]) for v in gates], 4), " new c =", np.round(c, 4), " new h =", np.round(h, 4))

# ---- 2. how much gradient survives T steps? product of Jacobians dh_t/dh_(t-1), for a plain RNN and an LSTM
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 16
def rnn_norms(rho, T=100):
    U = rng.normal(size=(n, n)); U *= rho / max(abs(np.linalg.eigvals(U)))      # scale to spectral radius rho
    Wx = rng.normal(0, 0.5, (n, n)); h = np.zeros(n); J = np.eye(n); out = []
    for t in range(T):
        h = np.tanh(U @ h + Wx @ rng.normal(size=n))
        J = (np.diag(1 - h ** 2) @ U) @ J                                       # chain rule, one factor per step
        out.append(np.linalg.norm(J, 2))
    return np.array(out)
def lstm_norms(T=100, forget_bias=1.0):
    W = rng.normal(0, 0.5, (4 * n, n)); U = rng.normal(0, 0.5 / np.sqrt(n), (4 * n, n)); b = np.zeros(4 * n); b[n:2 * n] = forget_bias
    h, c = np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n); J = np.eye(2 * n); out = []
    def step(state, x):
        return np.concatenate(lstm_step(x, state[:n], state[n:], W, U, b)[:2])
    for t in range(T):
        x = rng.normal(size=n); s = np.concatenate([h, c]); s2 = step(s, x)
        Jt = np.zeros((2 * n, 2 * n))
        for k in range(2 * n):                                                    # numerical Jacobian of one step
            e = np.zeros(2 * n); e[k] = 1e-6
            Jt[:, k] = (step(s + e, x) - step(s - e, x)) / 2e-6
        J = Jt @ J; h, c = s2[:n], s2[n:]; out.append(np.linalg.norm(J, 2))
    return np.array(out)
print("\nlargest singular value of the product of state Jacobians (d h_T / d h_1 for the RNN, d(h,c)_T / d(h,c)_1 for the LSTM)")
print("   T   RNN rho=0.9  RNN rho=1.2   LSTM b_f=1   LSTM b_f=5")
r09, r12, l1, l5 = rnn_norms(0.9), rnn_norms(1.2), lstm_norms(forget_bias=1.0), lstm_norms(forget_bias=5.0)
for T in (1, 10, 25, 50, 100): print(f"{T:4d}   {r09[T-1]:11.2e} {r12[T-1]:12.2e} {l1[T-1]:12.2e} {l5[T-1]:12.2e}")
print("cell-state path only: product of forget gates 0.95^50 =", round(0.95 ** 50, 4), " 0.99^50 =", round(0.99 ** 50, 3), " 0.999^50 =", round(0.999 ** 50, 3))

# ---- 3. a linear recurrence h_t = a_t*h_(t-1) + b_t can be computed in parallel: the pairs compose associatively
T = 8; a = rng.uniform(0.5, 1.0, T); bb = rng.normal(size=T)
seq = np.zeros(T); h = 0.0
for t in range(T): h = a[t] * h + bb[t]; seq[t] = h                              # sequential: T dependent steps
A, B = a.copy(), bb.copy(); step = 1
while step < T:                                                                   # scan: log2(T) rounds, each fully parallel
    A2, B2 = A.copy(), B.copy()
    A2[step:] = A[step:] * A[:-step]; B2[step:] = A[step:] * B[:-step] + B[step:]
    A, B = A2, B2; step *= 2
print("\nparallel scan equals sequential recurrence:", np.allclose(seq, B), " (rounds needed:", int(np.ceil(np.log2(T))), "instead of", T, ")")
k = 0.9 ** np.arange(6); u = rng.normal(size=6); y = np.zeros(6); h = 0.0
for t in range(6): h = 0.9 * h + u[t]; y[t] = h
print("linear state-space model = convolution with kernel", np.round(k[:4], 3), "...:", np.allclose(y, np.convolve(u, k)[:6]))

# ---- 4. attention: weights over three encoder states
scores = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 0.1]); alpha = np.exp(scores) / np.exp(scores).sum()
H = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
print("\nattention weights", np.round(alpha, 3), " context vector", np.round(alpha @ H, 3))

# ---- 5. parameter counts (PyTorch stores two bias vectors per gate group)
m_in, n_h = 300, 512
print("LSTM:", 4 * (n_h * (m_in + n_h) + 2 * n_h), " GRU:", 3 * (n_h * (m_in + n_h) + 2 * n_h), " plain RNN:", n_h * (m_in + n_h) + 2 * n_h)
try:
    import torch
    print("torch LSTM params:", sum(p.numel() for p in torch.nn.LSTM(m_in, n_h).parameters()), " GRU:", sum(p.numel() for p in torch.nn.GRU(m_in, n_h).parameters()))
except ImportError:
    print("(torch not installed - skipped cross-check)")

What to look for.

  1. Section 1 prints gates i, f, g, o = 0.8022, 0.9047, 0.978, 0.8249, new c = 1.6892 and new h = 0.7705: the table of the lesson.
  2. Section 2 prints the largest singular value of the product of state Jacobians after T steps. Expect roughly: plain RNN with spectral radius 0.9 — 2×10⁻⁴ at T = 10, 2×10⁻²² at 50, 8×10⁻⁴⁵ at 100; the same with radius 1.2 still vanishing because tanh saturates (7×10⁻²⁹ at 100); LSTM with forget bias 1 — 0.28, 1.4×10⁻⁸ and 3×10⁻¹⁶; LSTM with forget bias 5 — about 1.5 at every distance up to 100. The forget-gate bias is the difference between an LSTM that remembers and one that does not; try biases of 0, 2 and 3. The last line of the section shows the cell-path arithmetic: 0.95⁵⁰ = 0.077, 0.99⁵⁰ = 0.605.
  3. Section 3 shows the sequential recurrence and the scan agreeing (True) with 3 rounds instead of 8, and that a linear state-space model with a = 0.9 equals convolution with the kernel (1, 0.9, 0.81, 0.729, …).
  4. Section 4 gives attention weights (0.659, 0.242, 0.099) and the context vector (0.758, 0.341).
  5. Section 5 gives LSTM 1,667,072 and GRU 1,250,304 parameters at input 300, hidden 512 (with two biases per gate group, as PyTorch stores them; the textbook single-bias counts are 1,665,024 and 1,248,768); PyTorch agrees when installed.

Try next. Sweep the forget-gate bias from 0 to 6 and plot the gradient gain at T = 50; add a GRU cell and measure its gain; replace tanh by ReLU with an identity-initialised recurrent matrix (the "IRNN" trick) and observe the gain; implement teacher-forced training of a tiny character-level LSTM on a short text with hand-written BPTT.
recap: A recurrent network reads a sequence one element at a time, updating a hidden state h_t = tanh(W·x_t + U·h_(t−1) + b) with the same weights at every step, so its parameter count is independent of sequence length and it can process any length.

Training unrolls the network over time and backpropagates through it (BPTT); the gradient reaching step 1 from step T is a product of T − 1 Jacobians, so it vanishes or explodes exponentially: in the scalar example with recurrent weight 0.8, ∂h_T/∂h_1 was 0.52 after 3 steps, 0.096 after 10, 0.010 after 20 and 1.3×10⁻⁵ after 50.

An LSTM adds a cell state updated additively, c_t = f_t ⊙ c_(t−1) + i_t ⊙ g_t, with sigmoid gates f, i, o (forget, input, output) and a tanh candidate g; the gradient along the cell path is the forget gate, which can stay near 1, so long-range memory is learnable.
One LSTM step worked by hand with x = 2, h = 0.5, c = 1: gates i = 0.802, f = 0.905, g = 0.978, o = 0.825; new c = 0.905 + 0.785 = 1.689 and new h = 0.825 · tanh(1.689) = 0.770.

An LSTM with input size m and hidden size n has 4(n(m + n) + n) parameters (1.665 million for m = 300, n = 512); a GRU has three gate blocks instead of four (1.249 million); forgetting-gate biases are usually initialised positive.

Encoder–decoder models compressed a whole source sentence into one fixed vector, which limited long inputs; Bahdanau attention lets the decoder take a softmax-weighted sum of all encoder states at each step, and the transformer removed the recurrence entirely.

Recurrent models are inherently sequential in training (step t needs step t−1), which wastes GPU parallelism, and their fixed-size state limits exact recall; these are the two reasons transformers won, while their constant-size state and linear cost explain why recurrent ideas return.

A linear recurrence h_t = a·h_(t−1) + b_t can be computed as a convolution or with a parallel prefix scan in log T rounds; state-space models (S4, Mamba) and linear attention exploit this to train in parallel and run as recurrences at inference.

Practical rules: clip gradients, use truncated BPTT with detached state, mask padded positions in the loss and the recurrence, reset state between independent sequences, and never use a bidirectional RNN for left-to-right generation.
glossary: Averaged stochastic gradient descent: SGD that also keeps an average of the recent weights, used in AWD-LSTM.
A mechanism that lets a decoder form each step's context as a softmax-weighted sum of all encoder states instead of relying on one fixed vector.
ASGD Weight-Dropped LSTM (Merity et al., 2017): a heavily regularised LSTM language model that was state of the art before transformers and the base of ULMFiT.
Backpropagation applied to a recurrent network unrolled over its time steps; the gradient is summed over all steps that use each shared weight.
A decoding method that keeps the k highest-probability partial outputs at each step instead of only the single best.
Two recurrent networks reading a sequence in opposite directions, with their states combined, so each position sees both past and future.
Bilingual evaluation understudy: a score (0–100) of how much a machine translation overlaps with reference translations; higher is better.
The LSTM's internal memory, updated additively and protected by gates; the path along which gradients flow with gain f_t.
The original LSTM idea of a self-connected linear unit with weight 1, whose error signal neither vanishes nor explodes.
A loss that lets a recurrent model be trained on sequences whose input and output lengths differ and whose alignment is unknown, as in speech and handwriting.
A model in which an encoder network reads the input sequence into a representation and a decoder network generates the output sequence from it.
The mismatch between training with teacher forcing (true previous tokens) and inference (the model's own previous tokens).
An O(n log n) algorithm for converting a signal to the frequency domain, where convolution becomes multiplication.
A sigmoid gate f_t that multiplies the previous cell state, deciding how much of it to keep.
A learned vector of values between 0 and 1 (from a sigmoid) that multiplies a signal elementwise to let it through or block it.
Google's Neural Machine Translation system (2016): an 8-layer LSTM encoder–decoder with attention and residual connections.
Generative pretrained transformer: a decoder-only language-model family.
Graphics processing unit: the parallel processor used to train neural networks (gpu1).
Gated recurrent unit: a recurrent cell with an update gate and a reset gate and no separate cell state.
The vector a recurrent network carries from step to step as its summary of the sequence so far.
A sigmoid gate i_t that controls how much of the new candidate memory is written to the cell state.
A recurrent network with ReLU units whose recurrent matrix is initialised to the identity so the state is copied at initialisation.
The stored keys and values of all previous tokens that a transformer keeps during generation; it grows with context length.
A model that assigns probabilities to sequences, usually by predicting each token from the ones before it.
Long short-term memory: a recurrent cell with input, forget and output gates and an additively updated cell state.
Recent sequence models built on linear recurrences (structured state spaces, selective state spaces, receptance-weighted key-value) that train in parallel and run as RNNs.
A sigmoid gate o_t that controls how much of the (squashed) cell state is exposed as the hidden state.
An algorithm that evaluates an associative recurrence over T steps in about log₂ T parallel rounds.
A network that processes a sequence step by step, feeding its previous hidden state back in as an input.
The largest absolute eigenvalue of a matrix; for the recurrent weights it decides whether repeated multiplication grows or shrinks a vector.
A sequence model defined by a linear recurrence h_t = A·h_(t−1) + B·x_t with output y_t = C·h_t, computable as a convolution or a scan.
Training a decoder by feeding it the true previous token at each step instead of its own prediction.
Backpropagating through only the last k time steps, carrying the hidden state forward but detaching its gradient.
The Workshop on Machine Translation, whose yearly benchmark datasets (such as WMT'14 English–French) are standard translation test sets.
drill:
Work it out — size and steps

An LSTM layer with input size 300 and hidden size 512. Count its parameters and compare with a GRU. Then compute how many sequential steps a 2,048-token sequence needs, and contrast with a transformer.

Answer

Parameters. An LSTM has four blocks (forget, input, candidate, output), each a linear map over [x; h] with a bias: 4 × ((300 + 512) × 512 + 512) = 4 × (415,744 + 512) = 1,665,024 ≈ 1.67 M (PyTorch keeps two biases per block and reports 1,667,072). A GRU has three blocks: 3 × 416,256 = 1,248,768 ≈ 1.25 M, about 25% fewer. A plain RNN has one block: 416,256.

Sequential steps. 2,048: step t cannot begin until step t − 1 finishes, in both the forward and backward pass. A GPU with tens of thousands of cores sits almost idle, because the work is a chain of small matrix multiplications, not one big batch.

A transformer computes all 2,048 positions in parallel during training, because attention sees the whole sequence at once and causality is enforced by a mask rather than by ordering. That is the practical reason transformers scaled and RNNs did not: throughput, not expressiveness.

The nuance to add: at inference a transformer is also sequential, one token at a time, and must attend over the whole KV cache, about 0.5 MB per token for a 7B model. An LSTM of the same width and depth needs only 0.5 MB of state in total. State-space models (Mamba, S4) revive the recurrent formulation with a scan to try to get both.

Trace the gradient

A plain scalar RNN has recurrent weight u = 0.8 and, at the relevant steps, tanh slope factors of about 0.92 (states near 0.28). An LSTM cell-state path has forget gates of 0.95. Roughly how much gradient reaches 20 steps back in each, and what would you change to make the RNN remember?

Answer

RNN: the per-step factor is about 0.8 × 0.92 ≈ 0.74 (it varies with the state, with the exact recurrence in the lesson giving 0.010 at 20 steps). 0.74¹⁹ ≈ 0.003; the exact calculation gives about 0.01. Either way the gradient from 20 steps back is about 1% or less of what it would be with no decay.

LSTM cell path: 0.95¹⁹ ≈ 0.38 (about 0.36 for 20 factors): a third of the gradient survives, and a forget gate of 0.99 would keep 82%.

To make the plain RNN remember: you cannot fix it by initialisation alone. Options: initialise U near the identity or orthogonal so the gain is 1 (with ReLU units, the "IRNN" trick); use gradient clipping to control the explosive side; but the robust answer is to add the gate: switch to an LSTM or GRU and initialise the forget-gate bias to at least 1 so the cell remembers by default, or use a chrono initialisation matched to the dependency lengths. If the dependency is genuinely far (hundreds of steps) consider attention or a state-space layer.
qa: E
What is a recurrent neural network and why is it used for sequences?

An RNN reads a sequence one element at a time and carries a hidden state, a running summary of what it has seen: h_t = tanh(W·x_t + U·h_(t−1) + b). The same weights are used at every step, so the number of parameters does not depend on the sequence length and it can process inputs of any length, unlike a feed-forward network with a fixed input size. The final state can feed a classifier, or each step's output can predict the next token.
E
What are the gates of an LSTM and what does each do?

The forget gate f_t (a sigmoid) scales the old cell state, deciding how much memory to keep; the input gate i_t scales the new candidate memory g_t (a tanh) that is written; the output gate o_t decides how much of tanh(c_t) is exposed as the hidden state h_t. The cell state update c_t = f_t ⊙ c_(t−1) + i_t ⊙ g_t is additive, which is what lets information and gradients survive over many steps.
E
Why do plain RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies?

Backpropagation through time multiplies the gradient by the recurrent Jacobian (the weights times a tanh slope below 1) at every step, so over T steps it is scaled by roughly that factor to the power T. If the factor is below 1 the gradient vanishes and early inputs cannot influence learning; if above 1 it explodes. With recurrent weight 0.8 the gradient from step 1 to step 20 is about 0.01, and to step 50 about 10⁻⁵.
E
What is teacher forcing and what is exposure bias?

Teacher forcing trains a decoder by feeding it the true previous token at each step, which is fast and stable. At inference the decoder must consume its own previous predictions, which it never saw during training, so errors can compound; that mismatch is exposure bias. Mitigations include scheduled sampling, beam search, and sequence-level training objectives.
M
How does the LSTM avoid vanishing gradients, and where does it still fail?

The cell-state update is c_t = f_t ⊙ c_(t−1) + i_t ⊙ g_t, so ∂c_t/∂c_(t−1) = f_t: the gradient along the cell path is multiplied by a learned gate that can be close to 1 instead of by a weight matrix and a tanh slope. Over 50 steps a forget gate of 0.99 keeps 60% of the gradient. It still fails when gates are small (forget bias 1 gives 0.73 per step, 10⁻⁷ after 50 steps), because the gradient through the hidden-state path (via the gates' dependence on h) still vanishes, and because the fixed-size state limits how much it can remember. Measured LSTM language models use about 200 tokens of context.

Follow-up: Why initialise the forget-gate bias to a positive value? — With bias 0 the gate starts at 0.5 and the memory halves each step; a bias of 1–2 starts the cell remembering by default (Jozefowicz et al.).
M
Count the parameters of an LSTM layer with input size 300 and hidden size 512, and compare with a GRU.

Each of the four gate blocks has an input matrix (512 × 300), a recurrent matrix (512 × 512) and a bias (512): 512 · 812 + 512 = 416,256, so 4 × 416,256 = 1,665,024 (PyTorch, which keeps two bias vectors, reports 1,667,072). A GRU has three blocks: 3 × 416,256 = 1,248,768 (PyTorch 1,250,304), about 25% fewer. A plain RNN has one block: about 416 thousand.
M
Why can't an RNN be trained in parallel over time, and why does that matter?

The hidden state at step t depends on the state at step t−1, so step t cannot start until step t−1 finishes, in both forward and backward passes. A 2,048-token sequence needs 2,048 dependent small matrix multiplications, which leaves a GPU with tens of thousands of cores mostly idle. A transformer computes all positions at once as a few large matrix multiplies, with a causal mask enforcing order, so it uses the hardware fully. That throughput difference, more than expressiveness, is why transformers scaled to trillions of tokens and RNNs did not.

Follow-up: Can recurrences ever be parallelised? — Linear ones can: h_t = a_t h_(t−1) + b_t composes associatively, so a parallel prefix scan needs about log₂ T rounds; that is how state-space models and linear attention train in parallel.
M
What problem was attention originally invented to solve?

The fixed-size bottleneck in RNN encoder–decoders: the whole source sentence had to be squeezed into one vector, and translation quality dropped as sentences got longer. Bahdanau et al. (2014) let the decoder compute, at each output step, softmax weights over all encoder states and use their weighted sum as context. In their English–French experiments RNNsearch-50 scored 26.75 BLEU against 17.82 for the fixed-vector RNNencdec-50 on the full test set. The transformer came from noticing that with attention the recurrence was no longer needed.

Follow-up: How are attention weights computed? — A score (a small network or dot product) between the decoder state and each encoder state, then a softmax, e.g. scores (2, 1, 0.1) give weights (0.66, 0.24, 0.10).
M
How does truncated BPTT work and what are the trade-offs?

Instead of unrolling through the entire sequence, process it in chunks of k steps: run forward k steps, backpropagate through those k steps, then carry the hidden state into the next chunk but detach it so the gradient does not flow back further. Memory and compute per update become O(k) instead of O(T), and gradients over very long spans are bounded by the truncation, so dependencies longer than k are not learned directly. Choose k from the dependency lengths you need, carry (and reset between documents) state deliberately, and clip gradients.
H
Compare RNNs and transformers on training cost, inference cost and memory, and say what state-space models change.

Training: an RNN does O(T) sequential steps with no parallelism over time; a transformer does O(T²) attention work but in fully parallel matrix multiplies. Inference: an RNN updates a fixed-size state in O(1) per token with constant memory; a transformer attends over a KV cache that grows linearly (about 0.5 MB per token for a 7B model, equal to the size of an entire LSTM state of the same width and depth). State-space models such as S4 and Mamba keep the recurrent inference (linear time, constant memory) but use a linear recurrence, which can be computed as a convolution or a parallel scan in training, and Mamba makes the parameters input-dependent to do content-based selection; the paper reports 5× higher inference throughput than transformers and Mamba-3B matching transformers twice its size. The weak spot of any fixed-size state is exact recall of arbitrary earlier tokens, so hybrids keep some attention layers.

Follow-up: What is the link between linear attention and RNNs? — With a kernelised feature map, causal attention can be written as a recurrence on a matrix state S_t = S_(t−1) + φ(k_t) v_tᵀ, so a linear transformer is an RNN at inference (Katharopoulos et al., 'Transformers are RNNs').
H
Your LSTM language model trains but ignores context beyond a few dozen tokens. How do you diagnose and improve it?

First measure: shuffle or drop the distant context and see how perplexity changes (Khandelwal et al. found LSTM language models use about 200 tokens and sharply distinguish only the nearest 50). Check the gate statistics: forget gates saturated near 0 mean the cell forgets; check gradient norms across time, whether the state is being reset accidentally between chunks, and whether truncation length k is shorter than the dependencies. Fixes: positive forget-gate bias or chrono initialisation, longer truncation with state carry-over, layer normalisation and variational dropout (AWD-LSTM), gradient clipping, a larger hidden size, or adding attention or a memory (pointer) mechanism; if long context is the goal, a transformer or a hybrid with a state-space layer is the modern answer.

Christopher Olah — the canonical explanation; nearly every LSTM diagram descends from this post.
Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
Sutskever, Vinyals & Le, 2014 — a four-layer LSTM encoder–decoder reaching 34.8 BLEU on WMT'14 English→French, and the source-reversal trick.
Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
Bahdanau et al., 2014 — attention invented to fix the fixed-vector bottleneck; the direct ancestor of the transformer.
Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder-Decoder
Cho et al., 2014 — where the GRU comes from.
Wu et al., 2016 — an 8-layer LSTM encoder–decoder with attention and residual connections deployed at scale; 60% fewer translation errors than the phrase-based system.
The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks

t: Regularising deep networks: dropout, augmentation, early stopping
sum: Why deep networks overfit and what each regulariser assumes: dropout worked by hand (inverted scaling, test-time weight scaling, its link to adaptive L2, and the eval-mode bug), data augmentation and mixup, label smoothing, early stopping and weight averaging, and what changes in the LLM era.
prereq: ml2
Test error splits into bias, variance and noise; overfitting is high variance, where the model fits noise in the training set, and regularisation trades a little bias for a lot less variance.
ml3
Weight decay and L2 regularisation shrink weights toward zero; for plain gradient descent they are the same thing, and L2 is a ridge penalty in linear models.
dl4
BatchNorm behaves differently in training and evaluation mode and normalises with batch statistics, which interacts with anything that changes activation variance between the two modes.
dl5
AdamW applies weight decay directly to the weights, outside the adaptive step; PyTorch's train() and eval() switch the layers that behave differently at inference.
why:
You train a network on 30 noisy measurements of a smooth curve. After a few hundred steps its predictions track the true curve beautifully, and the error against it is the lowest it will ever be. You leave it running, because the training loss is still falling and loss falling is what training is for. By the end the training error is a sixth of the noise you know is in the data — the network has learned not just the curve but every random wobble in your 30 points — and its error against the true curve is six times worse than it was at step 450. Nothing went wrong in the code. The network did precisely what you asked: it minimised the training loss. The trouble is that minimising the training loss and predicting well on new data are different goals, and a deep network has enough capacity to pursue the first at the expense of the second.

This is overfitting, and the whole family of techniques for handling it is called regularisation: anything that makes it harder for a model to memorise the training set, or less rewarding, so that what it learns generalises. Modern networks make the problem sharp. They have millions or billions of parameters — often more than training examples — and in 2016 Zhang and colleagues showed that a standard image classifier can fit a dataset whose labels have been replaced by random noise perfectly. So capacity alone cannot explain why these networks generalise at all when the labels are real; a great deal of the answer is in how we train them, and regularisation is the part we control directly.

Regularisation is also where a lot of interview questions hide small, sharp bugs. What exactly does dropout do at test time, and why is the network scaled during training rather than after? What happens if you forget model.eval()? When does data augmentation hurt? Why has dropout largely disappeared from LLM pretraining but reappeared in fine-tuning? Answering well needs the mechanism, not the list of names, and the numbers: what dropout does to the sum of 100 activations, what a mixed image looks like, why early stopping and weight decay are close cousins.

This lesson builds the toolkit from the problem outward. We start with what overfitting looks like and what a training curve reveals, then set up a map of regularisers by what each one assumes. We work dropout by hand (masks, inverted scaling, backprop, the ensemble picture, the test-time weight-scaling rule with an exact worked example, and its equivalence to a data-dependent L2 penalty), including the inference-time bug. Then data augmentation and mixup, label smoothing, early stopping (with its link to weight decay) and weight averaging, and finally what regularisation looks like in the era of LLMs. The public case is the dropout paper itself, whose numbers we checked against the source, and the lab overfits a small network on purpose so that you can watch each regulariser change the curves.
body:
1. What overfitting is, with numbers

Recall from ml2 that expected test error splits into bias, variance and irreducible noise. Overfitting is high variance: the fitted function changes a lot if the training sample changes, because it is bending to fit the noise in this particular sample. The tell-tale gap between training and validation error is the generalisation gap. The lab makes it concrete. The training data are 30 points from y = sin(3x) + noise with noise standard deviation 0.3, so the noise variance is 0.3² = 0.09: no model can honestly get a mean squared training error below about 0.09. A network with two hidden layers of 64 tanh units, trained with Adam for 3,000 steps, reaches a training error of 0.016, more than five times below the noise floor, which is only possible by fitting noise. Its error against the true curve tells the rest of the story: 0.014 at step 450 (the best it ever does), 0.093 at step 3,000: overfitting made it more than six times worse.

The surprise of deep learning is that overfitting is not automatic in proportion to size. Zhang et al. (2017) trained standard architectures on CIFAR-10 with the labels replaced by random ones, and the networks still reached zero training error: "Deep neural networks easily fit random labels." So the networks could memorise everything, yet when the labels are real they generalise. Something in training (the optimiser's implicit preference for simple solutions, the structure of real data, architectural priors) does much of the regularising, and explicit regularisation adds to it. The consequence for practice is to treat regularisation as something you tune against validation curves rather than something you apply by reflex.

2. A map of regularisers

FamilyExamplesWhat it assumes or does
Penalty on weightsL2 / weight decay, L1, max-normSimpler functions have smaller weights
Noise in the networkDropout, DropConnect, stochastic depth, weight noiseRobust features survive random ablation; approximates averaging thinned networks
Noise in the data or targetsAugmentation, input noise, mixup, CutMix, label smoothingPredictions should be stable around each example, and labels are not perfectly certain
Limit the optimisationEarly stopping, small learning rate, fewer epochsWell-determined directions are learned first, noise later
AveragingEnsembles, EMA of weights, SWA, checkpoint averaging, TTAAveraging cancels idiosyncratic errors
StructureWeight sharing (CNNs), smaller models, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA)The right inductive bias; fewer free parameters
Prior knowledgePretraining and transfer (dl11)Features from a big dataset transfer to a small one

Two rules govern every entry. Each regulariser trades a little bias for less variance, so too much of it causes underfitting (the lab shows this below). And each rests on an assumption, so it helps only when the assumption is true of your data.

3. Dropout, step by step

The operation. For each unit in a layer, independently, with probability p set its output to zero ("drop" it); otherwise keep it. In inverted dropout, the standard implementation, the surviving outputs are also multiplied by 1/(1 − p) during training. Worked example with p = 0.5: activations (2, 4, 1, 3, 5) and a random mask (1, 1, 0, 1, 0) become (2, 4, 0, 3, 0) × 2 = (4, 8, 0, 6, 0). Dropped units are zero, survivors are doubled. Why double? Each unit is kept with probability 0.5, so its expected output is 0.5 × (2x) + 0.5 × 0 = x: the expected activation equals the original. With 100 units each equal to 1.0 the expected sum during training is 100 × 0.5 × 2 = 100, exactly the sum at inference when dropout is off and nothing is scaled. The lab confirms it (mean 100.04) and shows the price: the sum has a standard deviation of about 10. That noise is the regulariser; the matching mean is the reason inference needs no special code.

Backward. Dropout is a multiplication by a fixed (per-step) mask, so by the rules of dl1 the gradient flowing back is multiplied by the same mask and scale: dropped units receive gradient zero for this step, and survivors receive twice the usual gradient (for p = 0.5). Each step updates a different sub-network.

Why it works: three views.

  • Preventing co-adaptation. Without dropout, a hidden unit can learn to fix the mistakes of a specific neighbour, a fragile joint arrangement that fits the training data but breaks on new inputs. With dropout the neighbour is missing half the time, so each unit must be useful on its own. The dropout paper offers an evolutionary analogy: sexual reproduction mixes half of each parent's genes, so genes must work with many random partners rather than as a co-adapted set, and "ten conspiracies each involving five people is probably a better way to create havoc than one big conspiracy that requires fifty people to all play their parts correctly".
  • Implicit ensemble. A network with n units has 2ⁿ ways to keep or drop them (for 100 units, about 1.3 × 10³⁰), all sharing weights. Training with random masks trains an exponentially large ensemble of "thinned" networks, each getting occasional updates. Ensembles reduce variance; this one is essentially free.
  • Noise as a penalty. Injecting noise into a model is equivalent to adding a regularisation penalty; for a linear model dropout is exactly an L2 penalty with per-feature strengths (below).

The test-time rule and why it is right. The ensemble would need 2ⁿ forward passes; instead one runs the full network once with the weights scaled by the keep probability (in the original formulation; inverted dropout builds the scaling into training). This is a good approximation to averaging the sub-networks' predictions. For a single logistic unit it is exact in a precise sense. Take weights (2, 2), input (1, 1) and p = 0.5, with no train-time scaling. The four masks give pre-activations 0, 2, 2, 4, i.e. predictions σ(0) = 0.5, σ(2) = 0.881, σ(2) = 0.881, σ(4) = 0.982. Their arithmetic mean is 0.811. Their normalised geometric mean (the geometric mean of the probabilities, divided by the sum of the geometric means for the two classes) is 0.881, and the weight-scaled network gives σ(0.5 · 4) = σ(2) = 0.881: identical. (The geometric mean of sigmoids corresponds to averaging the logits, which is what scaling the weights does.) For deep non-linear networks the correspondence is approximate, but it works well in practice, and averaging many stochastic passes (MC dropout) is the more faithful version, used to estimate uncertainty.

Dropout as an adaptive L2 penalty. For linear regression with dropout on the inputs (each input kept with probability q and scaled by 1/q), the expected squared loss over masks is exactly

E[ ‖y − X̃w‖² ] = ‖y − Xw‖²  +  ((1 − q)/q) · Σⱼ wⱼ² · Σᵢ xᵢⱼ²

The second term is an L2 penalty on the weights, with a separate strength for each feature proportional to that feature's sum of squares (its variance, for centred data). So dropout shrinks weights attached to high-variance features more. The lab checks this numerically: with q = 0.8 and three features of scales 1, 3 and 0.3, the Monte Carlo average of the dropout loss was 103.81 and the formula gives 103.85. The penalty terms are 3.02, 3.28 and 0.85 for weights 0.5, −0.2 and 1.0: the small weight on the high-variance feature is penalised as heavily as the big weight on the low-variance one. That is a data-dependent ridge, which is what makes dropout different from plain weight decay.

Where dropout is used, and at what rate. Typical rates: 0.5 for fully connected hidden layers in the original paper (p = 0.5 for hidden units, 0.8 retention for input units), lower (0.1–0.3) for convolutional layers, where neighbouring activations are strongly correlated and dropping single pixels barely removes information. Variants adapted to structure: spatial dropout or DropBlock drop whole channels or contiguous regions; DropConnect drops weights rather than activations; variational dropout reuses one mask across all time steps of a sequence in RNNs (dl7) so the memory is not erased by fresh noise every step; stochastic depth (Huang et al., 2016) drops entire residual blocks with a survival probability that decays with depth — it took a 110-layer ResNet on CIFAR-10 from 6.41% to 5.25% error, with a theoretical saving of about 25% of training time, and let a 1,202-layer network reach 4.91%. In transformers dropout of about 0.1 is applied to attention weights, to each sub-layer's output before the residual addition, and to embeddings (the original transformer's base model used 0.1).

Interaction with BatchNorm. Dropout changes the variance of a unit's output between training (some units zeroed, others scaled up) and inference (no dropout). BatchNorm's running statistics (dl4) were collected under the training variance, so at test time a layer after dropout sees a different variance than BatchNorm expects. Li et al. (2018) call this "variance shift" and show it degrades accuracy when dropout comes before BatchNorm layers. Practical fixes: put dropout after the last BatchNorm, before the classifier, or use small rates. LayerNorm-based transformers do not have this problem.

4. The inference-time bug

Dropout and BatchNorm both behave differently in training and evaluation, and PyTorch switches them with model.train() and model.eval(). Forgetting eval() at validation or inference time is the most common evaluation bug in deep-learning code, and it has several distinct symptoms.

  1. Random predictions. Dropout stays on, so the same input gives different outputs on each call. The mean is right, the variance is not: 100 units of value 1.0 had a standard deviation of about 10 in their sum, and a classifier's top prediction can flip between calls.
  2. Batch-dependent normalisation. BatchNorm keeps using batch statistics instead of running averages (and updates the running averages with the validation batches, silently contaminating the model, dl4). Predictions depend on which other examples are in the batch, and a batch of one gives garbage.
  3. Metrics that are noisy and slightly off, easy to misread as a regularisation problem.

Related variants: applying the train-time scaling twice, or forgetting the test-time weight scaling in a hand-written non-inverted dropout, gives outputs of the wrong magnitude (twice too large or too small); leaving MC dropout switched on in a production endpoint gives non-deterministic results; and a library wrapper that calls train() on a sub-module after eval() on the parent re-enables dropout in part of the model. Defences: call model.eval() explicitly in the inference entry point, assert not model.training in serving code, and write a test that runs the same input twice and checks the outputs are identical. Finally, torch.no_grad() is an independent switch: it stops autograd recording (saving memory and time) and does nothing about dropout or BatchNorm; you need both, and forgetting eval() is a correctness bug while forgetting no_grad() is only a resource one.

5. Weight decay, briefly (see ml3 and dl5)

Weight decay shrinks every weight by a small factor each step, w ← (1 − lr·λ)w − lr·∇L; for plain gradient descent this equals an L2 penalty on the loss, and under Adam the decoupled form (AdamW) must be used (dl5). In the lab, decoupled weight decay of 1 (against a learning rate of 3×10⁻³) held the test error at 0.017 all the way to step 3,000, where the unregularised network had reached 0.093 — while a value of 10 was too strong (training error 0.176, well above the noise floor 0.09, test error 0.115): underfitting. With normalised layers weight decay controls the effective learning rate rather than capacity (dl4, dl5). LLM pretraining uses about 0.1 with AdamW.

6. Data augmentation

Data augmentation is regularisation by manufacturing training examples: apply transformations that do not change the label, so the model sees many variants of each example and must learn what is invariant. It is the strongest regulariser when the invariance is genuine, and it is the reason AlexNet could train a 60-million-parameter network on 1.2 million images: random 224×224 crops of 256×256 images plus horizontal flips "increases the size of our training set by a factor of 2048" (dl6), and PCA-based colour jitter added more. A second use is test-time augmentation (TTA): average predictions over several augmented copies of a test image (AlexNet used ten crops), a cheap ensemble.

Imagesrandom resized crops, flips, rotations, colour jitter, blur, Cutout / random erasing, mixup, CutMix, RandAugment / TrivialAugmentflips break digits and text; colour jitter breaks colour-defined labels; crops can remove the object

Mixup. Zhang et al. (2017) train on convex combinations of pairs of examples and of their labels: x̃ = λx₁ + (1 − λ)x₂, ỹ = λy₁ + (1 − λ)y₂, with λ drawn from a Beta(α, α) distribution. The figure shows λ = 0.7 blending two 3×3 "images" (a cat and a dog) into a new image and the soft label (0.7, 0.3). It encourages the network to behave linearly between training examples, which smooths decision boundaries, and it improves calibration and robustness to label noise. It is an instance of vicinal risk minimisation: train on samples from the neighbourhood of each training point rather than the points alone. The paper's numbers: CIFAR-10 test error 5.6% → 4.2% (PreAct ResNet-18), 3.8% → 2.7% (WideResNet-28-10), 3.7% → 2.7% (DenseNet-BC-190); CIFAR-100 25.6% → 21.1%, 19.4% → 17.5%, 19.0% → 16.8%. Cutout (mask a random square) and CutMix (paste a patch from another image and mix labels in proportion to the area) are related. RandAugment replaces a search over augmentation policies by two hyperparameters (how many transformations, how strong).

Pitfalls. Wrong invariances (above). Augmenting before splitting: if you create augmented copies and then split randomly into train and validation, near-duplicates of training images land in validation and inflate the score; always split first, then augment only the training part. Distribution mismatch: heavy augmentation makes training inputs look unlike test inputs; the model can be poor at clean test data (fixes: lighter augmentation at the end of training, or fine-tuning on clean data, as in the FixRes line of work).

7. Label smoothing

With one-hot targets and cross-entropy (dl1), the loss keeps decreasing as the correct-class probability approaches 1, which requires the correct logit to exceed the others by an ever larger margin: the model is pushed to be infinitely confident, and becomes over-confident and over-fitted. Szegedy et al. (2015) replace the target with a softened version: for K classes and smoothing ε, the true class gets 1 − ε + ε/K and every other class ε/K. With ε = 0.1 and K = 4 the target for class 0 is (0.925, 0.025, 0.025, 0.025) instead of (1, 0, 0, 0). Now the loss is minimised at a finite logit gap and confidence is capped (for K = 1,000 and ε = 0.1 the optimal probability on the true class is 0.9001, a logit gap of about ln(0.9001/0.0001) ≈ 9.1). They report "a consistent improvement of about 0.2% absolute" in both top-1 and top-5 error on ImageNet (Inception-v3). Label smoothing also improves calibration, and it makes the outputs less informative for distillation; it is standard in image classification and translation and rarely used in LLM pretraining.

8. Early stopping

Train while monitoring validation loss; keep the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss and stop after patience evaluations without improvement. It costs nothing, and the lab shows what it buys: the unregularised network's test error was 0.0139 at step 450 and 0.0929 at step 3,000, a gap of nearly 7×. Why it regularises: gradient descent from small weights fits the directions of high curvature (the signal, well determined by the data) first and the low-curvature directions (mostly noise) later. For a quadratic loss with curvature h along one direction, after τ steps at learning rate η the weight has reached the fraction 1 − (1 − ηh)^τ of its optimum, while ridge regression with strength λ reaches h/(h + λ). Matching them gives λ ≈ 1/(ητ). With η = 0.1 and τ = 100 (λ ≈ 0.1): for h = 1 the two fractions are 1.00 and 0.91; for h = 0.1, 0.63 and 0.50; for h = 0.05, 0.39 and 0.33; for h = 0.01, 0.095 and 0.091. The high-curvature directions are essentially fully learned, the low-curvature ones barely at all, exactly the shape of an L2 penalty. So early stopping is approximately weight decay in disguise, with the number of steps standing in for the penalty strength.

Practice and caveats. Evaluate on a validation set large enough to make its standard error small compared with the differences you care about (otherwise you overfit the validation set through the stopping rule); use patience to ride out noise; save the best checkpoint to disk. With a fixed learning-rate schedule such as cosine decay the last checkpoint is usually best, and early stopping is less used. And there are regimes where early stopping misleads: epoch-wise double descent (Nakkiran et al., 2019), where test error falls, rises, then falls again with longer training, and grokking (Power et al., 2022), where validation accuracy on small algorithmic tasks jumps from chance to perfect long after training accuracy has saturated, with weight decay driving the transition.

9. Averaging: EMA, SWA, ensembles

Noise in the final weights (from a high learning rate and mini-batch noise) hurts generalisation, and averaging removes it. Exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights, w_ema ← 0.999·w_ema + 0.001·w after each step, evaluated in place of the raw weights, is nearly free and standard in detection and diffusion models (dl10). Stochastic weight averaging (Izmailov et al., 2018) averages weights collected along the SGD trajectory with a constant or cyclical learning rate, giving flatter minima and better generalisation than the final iterate. Checkpoint averaging does the same across saved checkpoints. Ensembles of independently trained networks average predictions and are among the most reliable ways to improve accuracy and calibration, at N times the inference cost; distillation compresses an ensemble into one student.

The lab trains the same 64-unit network on the same 30 noisy points with different regularisers and measures the error against the true curve.

Read the table for the lessons. The moderate regularisers raise training error toward the noise floor (0.067–0.093 against 0.09) and lower test error by a factor of about five at the end of training: they stop the network memorising. The over-strong ones underfit: training error is far above the floor (0.176), so test error is bad for the opposite reason. Early stopping on the unregularised network matched the best regularised results (0.014 versus 0.013), but it required a validation set and a stopping rule, whereas the regularised nets were nearly as good with no stopping at all. And combining dropout with weight decay was worse than either alone, because together they over-regularised this tiny problem: regularisers add, they do not multiply the benefit.

11. Regularisation in the era of LLMs and fine-tuning

The regime decides. In LLM pretraining the dataset is so large that each token is seen about once, so there is little to memorise and the variance term is small; regularisation buys nothing and dropout costs capacity and compute, so modern recipes use dropout 0 (the original transformer's 0.1 is gone) and AdamW weight decay of about 0.1, whose role is mainly to control weight norms and the effective learning rate (dl4, dl5). When data is repeated, Muennighoff et al. (2023) measured the cost: "training with up to 4 epochs of repeated data yields negligible changes to loss compared to having unique data", with "meaningful gains from repeating data ... up to around 16 epochs beyond which returns diminish extremely fast". Fine-tuning on a small dataset is the opposite regime: overfitting is real, and the tools are small learning rates (10⁻⁵ to 5×10⁻⁵), one to three epochs, early stopping on held-out data, freezing lower layers or parameter-efficient methods (LoRA, whose adapters carry their own dropout of 0.05–0.1), mixing in general data or regularising toward the pretrained weights to prevent catastrophic forgetting, and, for instruction tuning, noise on the embeddings (NEFTune reports raising LLaMA-2-7B's AlpacaEval score from 29.79% to about 64.7% in the authors' Alpaca setting; treat as a result to reproduce). A modern twist: Liu et al. (2023), "Dropout Reduces Underfitting", show that dropout applied only during the early phase of training lowers the variance of mini-batch gradients and helps underfit models, and late-phase dropout helps overfit ones.
